# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3

Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.

One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

## Specimen

`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the
lines naming abc. `threads` holds 41 or more. Line 2 has a body, `open/m-41-2.md` beside it,
shown after it.

- m-41-0 2026-09-09T16:00:00Z from abc to def,ghi hello
- m-41-1 2026-09-09T16:05:42Z from ghi to abc hi
- m-41-2 2026-09-09T16:09:12Z from def to abc [hey, and the cycle that answers it](m-41-2.md)
- m-41-3 2026-09-09T16:12:30Z from abc done

  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

# Todo list

This file contains near term tasks with a short description and reference links to more details.
Its shape is [Todo format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format).

The other files:

- [BUGS.md](BUGS.md): List of vc-x1 bugs that should be addressed 
- [zDOING.md](zDOING.md): the cycle being worked on, its planning and its work's documentation,
  and the continuation notes a session leaves for the next.
- [zCLOSED.md](zCLOSED.md): the last finished cycle's record, kept until the next one closes.
- [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md): the bugs.

## Waiting

Important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on, in a form that can be
checked, and the rank it takes in `## Todo` once unblocked. Every opening checks each condition
and promotes what is met ([Opening](AGENTS.md#opening)).

- **Retire the frozen history: `notes/chores/` and `notes/done.md`.** (wink, 2026-08-27) They
  are frozen and no longer grow, and the agent-repo transcript plus git history hold what they
  hold. Delete both in one cycle, after a sweep turns every link into them (Todo entries, the
  backlog, rationale.md, the other members' messages) into a permalink at the SHA before the
  deletion.
  - Waits on: **`vc-x1 closed "<title>"`** landed, and the session viewer good enough to read
    a cycle's record from the transcript.
  - Place when unblocked: first.
- **Sync's remote look stops spawning git.** (wink + agent, 2026-10-09) Sync learns where a
  remote's bookmarks are by spawning `git ls-remote`, and downloads the commits of the ones that
  moved by spawning a `git fetch` that moves no ref, the sixth entry of the spawn register in
  `clippy.toml` and the one spawn of `git`. Replace `git_command` and its two callers in
  `src/jj/session.rs` with jj-lib's query, delete the `#[allow]`, and close the entry.
  - Waits on: jj-lib's public API offering that query. Neither 0.45.1 nor 0.46.0 has one:
    `rg -i 'ls.remote' src/` in the jj-lib source prints nothing, and its git subprocess layer is
    `pub(crate)`. An upstream feature request, once filed or found, is named here.
  - Place when unblocked: first, being one function.

## Todo

Entries are in priority order, the first highest, and reprioritizing is moving an entry. Each is a
`###` heading, so a citation is a link to its anchor. Long-tail entries live in
[todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the [Prose form](agent-data/prose.md#prose-form).
Deeper detail goes in a `notes/` design file (link via `[N]` ref).

### Improve init and add rename and delete subcommands

(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) A workspace's name is written into six places, and nothing renames or
removes them together: the work-repo's directory, the agent-repo's directory when it is not
nested, the two repos on the remote, each repo's `origin` URL, the `.vc-config.{toml|md}` of both
sides, and the Claude Code symlink. And `init` makes a workspace it cannot always finish, or that
Claude Code does not find.

- The order is wink's: `init` is fixed first, then `vc-x1 delete`, then `vc-x1 rename`. Each is a
  cycle of its own.
- The `init` work is more than one cycle, wink's order: the agent template `--use-template` looks
  for first, then the path over 200 characters, then the name GitHub would change, the order the
  three parts below are in.
- Delete is ahead of rename: its "find every part of a workspace from its config" is what rename
  reuses, and it gives `init` the cleanup it lacks.
- The parts are `####` headings, where [Todo format](agent-data/notes.md#todo-format) asks for

What is being done: the running cycle's planning and its work's documentation. The last
finished cycle's is in [zCLOSED.md](zCLOSED.md), and what we might do is in [TODO.md](TODO.md). The
block's shape is on trial: it opens with the Todo as it was picked from `TODO.md`, then the
Deliberation, the plan, Solution and Acceptance check, and the Ladder with its details.

This file is a trial (2026-10-09). The agent-files still name `TODO.md > ## In Progress` as the
record's home, and the cycle that makes this file the rule is [The cycle-record moves out of
TODO.md into zDOING.md](TODO.md#the-cycle-record-moves-out-of-todomd-into-zdoingmd).

## Continuation notes

Where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a record: read first, acted
on, and reset to `_None._` by the reader. Kept here by the trial and no longer in `TODO.md`,
where [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint) still says to look.

- 2026-10-21, late, wink stopping for the night. Rung **feat: vc-x1 install copies the release
  build** is `(current)` at 0.85.7-3, its work in the uncommitted `@` over the status rung's
  commit, 14 files. The last full validation passed, and the fast one passed after the last edit.
  "please review" was said, and wink has not said continue.
- wink's last words: "I'm not sure we're headed in the right direction to have vc-x1 be a build
  system." Start there, before any flip or description. The rung's review grew `install` into
  running `[build] release` first, `run` was planned to build first too, and `build` now says
  `built` or `up to date`. Whether vc-x1 should run builds at all, or only name and copy what
  cargo built, is open, and the answer may shrink this rung and reshape the run rung.
- What the review changed, all in `@` and in the rung's subsection and the Deliberation:
  - `[build]` is plain `cargo build`, `--release --locked` and `--locked`, the binaries in
    `target/release/vc-x1` and `target/debug/vc-x1`, no `--root`, "staged" gone from every doc.
  - `install` reports what it copies and refuses only a wrong copy, wink reversing the earlier
    refuse-on-failure say. It builds the release first, a no-op when nothing changed.
  - `-V` is read at its first version-shaped line, after wink's test `println!` was read as
    version `hi` and copied. The `println!` is removed.
  - The rung was retitled from "install deploys the staged release", the anchor with it.
  - Todo entries added: **A config file says what and its constraints, and the why is in the cycle
    record** and **The release stamp is reconsidered now that install builds**, both placed before
    **dr-1 is built in Rust**.
- After this rung, as planned: the inserted rung for **Every repo's .gitignore ignores .claude,
  and settings stay out of agent-repos**, then the run rung, then the closing. The closing's
  README guidance gains the first install by `cargo run --locked -- install`, and again whenever
  the installed `vc-x1` is too old for the workspace.
- Binaries: `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1` is wink's test install of 0.85.7-3, dirty, from this bookmark,
  and may still print a `wink:` line. `tmp/dev` and `tmp/rel` are gone, wink's deletes.
  `target/` was cleaned more than once tonight, so `target/debug/vc-x1` may be missing, and
  `cargo run --locked -- <command>` rebuilds it.

## In Progress

### feat: vc-x1 install stages, deploys, and runs builds

(wink + agent, 2026-10-21, opened 2026-10-21) The last two work rungs of **feat: vc-x1 commit,
install, and run-dev**, deferred at its closing, run as their own cycle and widened at the opening
into three stages, dev, release, and the PATH, each with its command. The keys that cycle landed
as `[install] release`, `dev`, and `dev-bin` were read by nothing, and become `[build]`'s here.

#### Problem

Land's promotion is a hand-typed `cargo install --path .`, which checks nothing: it installs
whatever the working copy holds, pushed or not, at a suffixed version or a bare one, and it
replaces the PATH binary in the same step that builds the release, so the release is first run
when it is already the one consumers get. The `build.rs` guard that once refused a suffixed
version under the plain name is gone, and could never see the bookmark or the remote. The dev
binary lives off the PATH under `tmp/dev`, reached only by typing its path, and nothing says when
it is stale. The table that names the builds is read by nothing.

#### Solution

Provisional, the plan as the install rung left it:

| Command | What it does | When |
|---|---|---|
| `vc-x1 validate` | fmt, clippy, every test | every rung, before review |
| `vc-x1 validate --fast` | the unit tests only | while iterating |
| `vc-x1 build-dev` | the dev build, into `target/debug` | to build without running |
| `vc-x1 run-dev` | `build-dev`, then runs it | trying the change |
| `vc-x1 build` | the release, into `target/release`, with its stamp | at Land, or to try the release profile |
| `vc-x1 run` | `build`, then runs it | the smoke check before install |
| `vc-x1 install` | `build`, then reports it and copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` | at Land |

- `vc-x1 build` runs `[build] release`, `cargo build --release --locked`, from any commit, and
  writes a stamp beside `[build] release-bin` naming the commit it was built from, the state of
  the source code that was compiled, and the binary's size and modification time.
  `vc-x1 build-dev` runs `[build] dev`, `cargo build --locked`. Neither checks anything, and
  neither touches the PATH.
- `vc-x1 install` runs `[build] release` as `build` does, a no-op when nothing changed, then copies
  `[build] release-bin` into `[install] dir`, `~` expanded, as a temporary file renamed into place,
  so the binary installed is the binary tested. It first reports what it copies: the version and
  commit the binary's `-V` shows, whether that commit is `main` and `main@origin`, its state, a
  suffixed version, and whether the stamp still matches the binary. It refuses only a copy that
  would be wrong: no binary, a binary whose `-V` will not run, or a missing install directory.
- `vc-x1 run` runs `build` and then `[build] release-bin`, and `vc-x1 run-dev` runs `build-dev`
  and then `[build] dev-bin`, as `cargo run` builds before it runs, each with the given arguments
  from any directory of the workspace, and each warning when the binary's `-V` is not the
  manifest's version.
- `vc-x1 validate` checks the source and makes no build: `[validate] full` loses the dev build's
  line.
- The schema's `[build]` table holds `release`, `release-bin`, `dev`, and `dev-bin`, and
  `[install]` holds `dir`. `vc-config-model.md` is regenerated, and this
  workspace's `.vc-config.md` carries the values.

#### Acceptance check

`build` leaves `target/release/vc-x1` and its stamp, `run -V` prints the manifest's version,
`build-dev` leaves `target/debug/vc-x1` at the manifest's version, and `run-dev -V` prints it.
`install --dry-run` with nothing built builds the release, and on the cycle's bookmark reports the
suffixed version, the commit off `main`, the dirty state, and a stamp that matches. This cycle's own
Land builds by the dev binary's `build`, smoke-tests by its `run -V`, and installs by its `install`,
the first install the command makes, its report showing `main` and `main@origin`, clean, and a bare
version.

#### Ladder

- [feat: vc-x1 install stages, deploys, and runs builds opening][0] (done)
- [feat: vc-x1 build stages the release][1] (done)
- [feat: status takes the write commands' scope][2] (done)
- [feat: vc-x1 install copies the release build][3] (current)
- [feat: vc-x1 run and run-dev run the builds][4]
- [feat: vc-x1 install stages, deploys, and runs builds closing][5]

##### feat: vc-x1 install stages, deploys, and runs builds opening

The cycle's setup commit: create and publish the bookmark at `main`, move the Todo entry into this
block, widened to three stages, and bump the version-of-record. Under the bend above it renames
nothing, and it makes the dev build a debug build, so the cycle's validations run on it.

##### feat: vc-x1 build stages the release

The release is built under its own root with a stamp naming the commit it came from, so it can be
run before anything on the PATH is replaced, and `build-dev` is the dev build on demand.

- `vc-x1 build` runs `[build] release`, now `--root tmp/rel`, and writes the stamp beside the new
  `[build] release-bin`, recording the commit, the state of the source code that was compiled,
  and the binary's size and modification time. The old stamp is removed before the build and the
  new one written only once it passes and the binary is there, so no stamp outlives a failed
  build.
- `vc-x1 build-dev` runs `[build] dev` and writes no stamp.
- Both builds' commands, and `validate`'s, get the commit and the state in their environment, and
  vc-x1 compiles them in, so its banner carries the commit as build metadata and `vc-x1 version`
  a `build` line, wherever the binary is copied.
- `build.rs` falls back to git's `HEAD` when no variables are passed, so a hand-typed cargo build
  reports its commit too, marked `.unknown`. The `HEAD` reader is its own file, compiled by
  `build.rs` and by the crate's tests.
- The names: the rung began as `install` with `--dev`, the dev build became `install-dev`, and
  both became `build` and `build-dev`, `install` kept for the step onto the PATH. The table is
  `[build]`, its keys the ones the last cycle landed under `[install]`.
- `[validate] full` no longer builds the dev binary, which `run-dev` will build first.

content.text:
I couldn't confirm the reason you remember from the record. This cycle's Deliberation gives a different reason for the change: a hand-typed `cargo install --path .` checks nothing. It doesn't check whether the work is pushed, whether the version still has a suffix, or whether the binary installed is the one that was tested. My Bash mistakes aren't mentioned. They may be recorded in an earlier cycle or in the agent-repo's transcripts. Either way, I think it's a real risk, and it supports the change.

On Python versus Bash: I can't measure how often I've used each across sessions. But I don't think switching languages fixes the mistake.
- The mistake is a habit: I send output to a file and never read it, or I hide a command's exit status.
- In Python I can run a command without `check=True`, write its output to a file, and carry on just as easily.
- The deeper problem is that I write a new script for each Land. Nobody reviews it, and it's slightly different every time, so each Land is a fresh chance to get it wrong.
- A committed command is written once, reviewed, and tested, and it does the same thing every time. That's why `install` should exist, not because Bash is error-prone.

On whether vc-x1 is becoming a build system, I'd separate two things it does:
- **Running the configured build commands:** this isn't a build system. `install` runs the `[build] release` list the same way `validate` runs `[validate] full`. vc-x1 doesn't know how to build anything, because cargo does the building. I'd keep this.
- **Tracking whether a build is stale:** the stamp file, and `build` comparing the binary's size and time to say `built` or `up to date`. This part is a build system, and cargo already does it. The commit compiled into the binary, which its `-V` reports, already says where a binary came from.

My recommendation:
- Keep `build`, `run`, `run-dev` and `install` as thin wrappers around the config's command lists.
- Have `install` keep its checks and its report: the commit against `main` and `main@origin`, clean or dirty, a version with a suffix, and the copy that renames into place.
- Take the stamp out, and the `built`/`up to date` message with it. That settles the existing Todo entry **The release stamp is reconsidered now that install builds**.

This rung would get somewhat smaller, and the run rung would stay as planned.

The plain version: the real fix for my mistakes is a reviewed command that does the Land steps the same way every time, whatever language it's written in. vc-x1 should run cargo and check the result, but not try to work out when a rebuild is needed, because cargo already does that.

Do you want me to take the stamp out in this rung, or keep it as it is and leave that to the Todo entry?

### Local ladders

Retired name: "Ladder (sub-cycle)", which collided with the working record's `#### Ladder`. That
ladder is the cycle's rung list, and a local ladder is one rung's scratch history. The fast
validation per ladder commit is non-negotiable because a regression in an early ladder commit
otherwise goes uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising bisection cost. The
scratch `jj describe` is the one permitted describe because the commit is never published and never
carries a trailer.

## Working practices

**One command per shell invocation** because bundling hides which step produced which output.

**Never mask a command's exit status**: a pipeline's status is the last command's, so a validating
command piped into `tail` / `grep` reports the filter's success, not its own. A trailing
`; echo "exit=$?"` prints the status while the invocation itself still exits 0, so the failure is
visible only to whoever reads the text. `failed=$rc` stays unquoted because it has no spaces to
protect, and the quotes can stop a harness permission rule from matching a command it would
otherwise allow (wink, 2026-08-05).

**Use https remotes, not ssh.** Unconditional rather than "when the agent is sandboxed" because the
remote is chosen at clone time and whether a sandboxed agent will ever touch the repo is not
knowable then. A sandbox denies ssh twice over: reads of `~/.ssh` are blocked except the signing key
and `known_hosts`, so no auth key is available, and we think a host allowlist cannot admit port 22
at all, since ssh carries no SNI or Host header to match on. The network leg is a spawned `git`
child that inherits the sandbox, which is why the same config succeeds from a human's terminal and
fails from a session. Both wrong theories (size, timeouts) were held, and eliminated by test, before
the rule was written. Changing a remote's URL needs the user's go because it moves where the repo
publishes.

**Delegate mechanical subtasks to lesser models** because top-model tokens are the scarce resource.
**Don't use the per-project memory directory** because easy for everyone to find beats convenient
for the agent alone. **Mark speculation** so a reader can tell the measured from the inferred.

content.content:
### Pushing

_None recorded._

#### Policy

**Delegation waives stops, never flow**, because the stops are the synchronous half of review and
the flow (the records, the validation, the bookmark discipline) is what deferred review reads. A
delegated cycle that skipped a record would leave the deferred reviewer nothing to read.

#### Before any push

**Every push needs approval** because a push publishes, and what is published is corrected only by
a coordinated force-push of history someone else may already hold. Approval is the one moment the
user can still say no at no cost.

#### At rest: push, stop, squash-push

The agent-repo is a live journal, so everything after a `vc-x1 push` invocation, its own
record and any closing words, lands in the agent-repo's `@` as a trailing tail. That tail is why the
agent cannot squash-push the agent-repo: the squash-push is itself an action that adds to the tail,
so it never reaches a fixed point. Thus the user must do the squash-push in the agent-repo anytime
the agent acts visibly or behind the scenes. Importantly, a squash-push does not alter the change id
in the agent-repo commit, so the `ochid` in the work-repo commit continues to resolve.

### Close-out

### Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)

**Trailers are stamped by push, never hand-written**, because the change id a trailer names does
not exist until push makes the paired commit: an agent-repo ochid names `@-` after the push, and an
unpushed `@` gets a fresh chid in every clone ([Resolvability](jj.md#resolvability)). A trailer
written by hand is at best a guess at that id, and a wrong one breaks the only join between the two
histories.

### Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer

**A re-describe is coordinated** because it is a history rewrite that silently drops the cross-repo
link: the `ochid:` trailer lives in the description, and a new description without it leaves the
paired commit pointing at nothing. Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer
survived only by being copied across by hand.

### Cycle bookmarks: create and land

**The rule and the commands are separated** because the commands are the part expected to change:
we think a `vc-x1 start-change <bookmark>` will eventually own the create half, replacing the
create bullets and nothing else, while the rule in AGENTS.md stays as it is.

## Sync

One section holds the command (wink, 2026-10-13) because it is run at several steps, and a
command written three times is changed in two. The steps are the ones that depend on `main`: an
acquaint reads the records a stale `main` holds, an opening creates the cycle's bookmark on it, a
rung is built on it, and Land moves it.

- Acquaint looks and does not sync so that "left as found" has no exception: the user hears of a
  repo that is behind before anything moves. The first form was a `jj git fetch` and a look, and
  the look-only sync replaced it since it reports what a sync would do.
- Opening syncs because an acquaint's look is as old as the session. A cycle opened hours into
  one, or the second cycle of a session, would create its bookmark on a `main` the remote may
  have moved past, the failure the acquaint's check was written for, reached by a later door.
  "Whatever the cycle's form" is there so a lightweight cycle's first commit and a single-step
  cycle's one commit owe it too.
- Land syncs because `main` is the one target someone else can reach first, a cycle's other
  pushes going to its own bookmark. A `main` that moved stops the Land because the tree that
  would land is no longer the one reviewed and validated, and its version-of-record was bumped
  from a `main` since passed. How to recover is left to the first time it happens.
- The flags `--force` and `--rebase` are the user's because sync holds a repo back exactly when
  following the remote would tangle local work, and overriding that is a rewrite.
- A rung syncs at its step 0 (wink, 2026-10-15) because a rung's start is the cheapest moment to
  take in a moved `main`: the working copy is empty, a rebase of the bookmark carries only pushed
  rungs, and the sync never moves the bookmark, so it cannot hurt the rung. The closing's is
  required because its record and version are what lands, and the opening's is the opening's
  first step already.
  - The moment weighed first was before the push, since every push lands on the agent-repo's
    `main` directly, the agent-repo having no bookmark. Step 0 leaves a long rung's push open to
    an agent-repo `main` moved meanwhile, a cost accepted: one session writes the agent-repo, so
    its remote rarely moves, and a re-run push is safe.
- A rung's sync between is optional, the agent's or the user's call, because a rung pushes to its
  own bookmark and Land catches a moved work-repo `main` anyway, so it buys only an earlier
  warning, worth having on a long cycle or with another session pushing. "When a repo has not
  been synced in a while" was weighed as a required moment and left out, "a while" being nothing
  an agent can check.
- The cycle's bookmark is looked at and never synced because a rebase of a pushed bookmark is a
  remote rewrite at its next push.

## Cycle protocol
### Close-out

Each close-out step exists because a close-out once went wrong without it.

- The finished block moves to `## Closed` so the finalized record exists in a tree
  ([Cycle-record](#cycle-record)).
- It asks what must outlive the cycle because the block is replaced one opening later, and the
  rung-time rule (a design finding goes to `notes/` by the rung that made it) relies on noticing in
  the moment.
- A closed block is never amended because its tree is the landmark's, and a rewrite there is a
  rewrite of published history.
- The user restarts the agent after the close-out (wink, 2026-08-24) because context degrades over
  a long session, nothing is in flight once the cycle has landed, and an agent cannot restart
  itself, so the step says what must be written down before the exit.
- The size row is recorded only when an agent-file changed (wink, 2026-09-16) because the table
  is the count's history, and a row repeating the last one records nothing.
- The `(current)` / `(done)` markers stay in the closed block (wink, 2026-08-28) because they have
  value: the finished block is the ladder as it was worked, and a closed block is one every rung of
  which reads `(done)`, so a rung reading otherwise is a finding. The earlier "drop the markers"
  step was one more transform of the record, of the kind [Cycle-record](#cycle-record) retired.
- The single-step case is spelled out because a single-step close-out went wrong when it was left
  to analogy (2026-08-26): the agent treated the one commit as a closing rung.
  - The agent-repo commit took the title plus " closing" while the work-repo commit kept the bare
    title, and the agent-repo held two commits for the one rung, so the `ochid:` trailers did not
    match.
  - The In Progress block was deleted rather than moved, so the cycle reached neither
    `notes/chores/` nor `## Done`.
  - The repair was a hand re-describe and squash.
- Pushed titles keep their names through a rename (2026-09-05) because the sync step said only
  "sync the title if the scope shifted", and a mid-cycle rename of the benches met three pushed
  rung titles and a bookend pair on the old name. Retitling a pushed commit is a re-describe of
  a published one, so the sync can reach the block's text and the unpushed rungs and nothing

content.content:
## Rules

The rules are an index, seventeen bullets, each a one-sentence summary and a link to the section
that states the rule, so a rule lives in one place and a citation points there. Until 2026-08-27
each rule was a numbered heading in AGENTS.md with one line and a link, 82 lines that read as
spread out rather than as a list, and every rule had a mirror heading here, eleven of them
`_None recorded._`. The names stay, since a review cites a rule by name. The sentence stays too
(2026-08-28): AGENTS.md is in the agent's context every turn and the linked section is not, and a
bare name reminds an agent of a rule it holds without stating one it does not, so the sentence is
what the agent checks against. Bullets, not numbers, since the rules are unordered and numbering
bred "hard rule N" citations that broke on every renumber. Flat, not grouped by file
(2026-08-28): each bullet's link already shows the file, so a per-file header repeated it and cost
a nesting level, and the order alone keeps this file's rules ahead of the outer files'. A section
that has a why links it at its head, so the index carries none.

A bend's record names its scope (2026-09-05) because a scoped waiver, "complete it as you see fit"
over a whole cycle, left the agent to decide alone whether Land was inside it. It decided not, and
the decision was right, but a rule that makes the agent draw that line is a rule that will be drawn
differently next time.

## Terminology

**Retired names.** "Bot repo" (2026-08-21), when the code respelled the side `agent`. "Instruction
files", an earlier name for the agent-files. "Ladder (sub-cycle)" for a local ladder, under [Local
ladders](#local-ladders). "Project layer" (2026-10-18), the project's own agent-files, retired when
the one file it named became local ([custom.md](#custommd)).

## The dual-repo model

content.text:
You're right that it goes back a long way. I didn't find the exact `> xxx` episode written down anywhere. I searched `rationale.md`, `notes/`, and the frozen `notes/chores/` history. It may only be in the agent-repo transcripts. But `rationale.md` does record the same kind of mistake more than once, and they're months apart:

- **Never mask a command's exit status** (Working practices, from 2026-08-05). This covers piping a validating command into `tail` or `grep`, or adding a trailing `; echo "exit=$?"`. In both cases the invocation exits 0, so "the failure is visible only to whoever reads the text." That's the same failure as capturing output to a file and not reading it: the command reports success and the result goes unchecked.
- **A failure is read before validation runs again** (The per-rung flow, 2026-10-15). A full validation failed. I re-ran it, the second run passed, and I reported the pass as the result without naming why the first run failed. The cause turned out to be a race between tests.

Both are about how I handle a command's result, and neither depends on the language. A Python `subprocess.run` without `check=True` whose output goes unread is the same mistake. I don't think the recent shift toward Python retires the concern. I can't measure how often it happens now, and the record shows it has kept coming back over months.

That pattern also answers the build-system worry. The project's remedy so far has been a command that does the sequence and checks the result itself. `vc-x1 validate` is one: it runs the list, stops at the first failure, and exits non-zero, so there's no output for me to forget to read. `install` and `run` do the same for Land: they run the configured commands, check what came out, and refuse or report. vc-x1 isn't working out how to build anything; cargo still does that.

So my recommendation from before stands, with that as the stated reason:
- Keep `build`, `run`, `run-dev`, and `install` as runners of the config's command lists that check the results.
- Drop the stamp and the `built`/`up to date` size-and-time comparison. That part repeats cargo's own staleness tracking, and it's the one piece that does make vc-x1 a build system.

If you agree, I'll also add a line to the Deliberation recording this reason for keeping the builds in vc-x1.

The plain version: the record shows the mistake is ignoring a command's result, whatever the language. The fix the project already uses is a command that checks the result for me, and `install` is that fix applied to Land. The only piece that is really a build system is the stamp, which repeats work cargo already does.

Shall I take the stamp out in this rung, or leave it for its Todo entry?

# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

## A bookend

Title: `refactor: extract config loader opening`

```
Opens the cycle "refactor: extract config loader". Its record is the
In Progress block in TODO.md.
```

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the
cycle by its title and pointing at its record. The closing's body is the same shape with "Closes".
feat: status takes the write commands' scope

Status parsed its scope on its own, long names, a positional, and comma
forms, while the write commands took w, a, b, and p through a bare
function that gave tab completion nothing to offer.

Solution: one builder makes each command's -s parser from the scopes it
offers, so status takes the write commands' four and every -s completes
exactly what its command takes, a scope it does not offer still parsing
to reach the command's own refusal. Status's positional and comma forms
are gone, a plain repo is -s p, and the Todo gains an entry for shell
completion asking the binary typed. See details in zCLOSED.md.

ochid: /.claude/kqouqytkvsso

-----
feat: vc-x1 build stages the release

Land's promotion is a hand-typed cargo install that checks nothing,
puts the release on the PATH in the same step that builds it, and
leaves no record of the source code it was built from.

Solution: vc-x1 build stages the release under its own root with a
stamp naming its commit, the state of the source code that was
compiled, and the binary's size and time, and vc-x1 build-dev builds
the dev binary under another, neither touching the PATH. Every build
carries its commit and state in its banner, validate now only checks
the source, and status takes the short scope forms. See details in
zCLOSED.md.

content.content:
### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
  to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
  form, the general form at its smallest.
- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.

**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.

Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit).

vc-x1 0.85.7-3+38a446f041da.dirty

Commit the working copies as a rung's pair, one commit per repo of a
dual workspace, each stamped with the other's change id, before
anything is pushed.

The pair is what the per-rung flow reviews, description and diff
together, by `jj show @-` in either repo. A fix after the review folds
into the pair, never a remote rewrite, and `vc-x1 push` publishes what
was reviewed.

-s is required: `b` makes both commits now, `w` the work half with
the agent half left to push, `p` commits a plain repo with no
trailer, and `a` is refused, an agent commit made first being
unpaired. -R is optional and says where. --body is the text, or
@PATH to read it from a file.

Usage: vc-x1 commit [OPTIONS] --scope <SCOPE> --title <STR> --body <STR|@PATH>

Options:
  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s b|w`, its root or either repo,
          or the repo itself for `-s p` [default: the current directory]

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
vc-x1 0.85.7-3+38a446f041da.dirty

Publish a rung's pair: the work commit on its bookmark and the
agent commit on `main`. Push carries no description and writes
none, so what was reviewed is what goes out.

`commit` makes the pair, both commits now (-s b) or the work
half with its trailer naming the agent @ (-s w). Push refuses a
work @ that is not empty, unsquashed work being a fix to fold
or the next rung, and a work @- with no `ochid:` trailer, which
is not a pair's commit.

The halves are independent, each trailer being fixed before
push runs, so -s b is -s a then -s w, the order the pair is
completed in:
  - agent  complete the partner by the state found: fold the
           journal into a committed one, or commit it as the
           partner when pending or the agent repo changed;
           then squash-push main
  - work   restamp the unpublished work commit if its trailer
           does not name the partner, then set and push
           <bookmark>

-s is required: `b` both halves, `a` the agent half, `w` the work
half, `p` a plain repo's @- on its bookmark. -R is optional and
says where. The bookmark is the line's unless named as a check.

Rerunning is always safe: a half whose work is done finds nothing
to do. A half that fails before its own push restores the repo it
touched via `jj op restore`.

## build.release

The release build: the commands that build the artifact, in order, each element one invocation whose
exit status is checked, leaving the binary where it can be run before anything on the PATH is
replaced, `target/release` for a plain `cargo build --release`. `vc-x1 build` runs it from any
commit, and writes a stamp beside [build.release-bin](#buildrelease-bin) naming the commit it was
built from. `vc-x1 install` runs it too, before it copies the binary at a cycle's Land. Its commands
run with `VC_X1_BUILD_COMMIT` and `VC_X1_BUILD_STATE` in their environment, the same facts, for an
artifact that compiles them in, as [build.dev](#builddev)'s and the `[validate]` lists' do. Owned by
the work side because it builds the artifact.

```toml
[build.release]
homes = ["workspace-code"]
kind = "str-list"
doc = "The release build, in order, one invocation per element, run by `vc-x1 build`"
used-by = "vc-x1 build and vc-x1 install"
example = ["cargo build --release --locked"]
```

## build.release-bin

The binary the release build leaves, relative to the config file's directory, or as is when
absolute. vc-x1 never works it out, from cargo or from the package's name: the release build's
commands decide where the binary goes, so the config says. `vc-x1 build` writes its stamp beside it,
the path with `.stamp` appended, holding the full commit id of `@-` the build was made from,
`state`, the state of the source code that was compiled, `clean` when `@` was empty so the code is
exactly that commit and `dirty` when `@` held edits that were compiled too, and the binary's size
and modification time, so a binary rebuilt by hand after `vc-x1 build` is told from the one it made.
Required by `vc-x1 build` and `vc-x1 install`.

```toml
[build.release-bin]
homes = ["workspace-code"]
kind = "str"
doc = "The release build's binary, beside which `vc-x1 build` writes its stamp"
used-by = "vc-x1 build and vc-x1 install"
example = "target/release/vc-x1"
```

cycle builds replaces the `vc-x1` on the PATH until the cycle lands. Both are `--locked`, so they
compile the same dependencies, the ones `Cargo.lock` commits:

- Dev: `vc-x1 build-dev` runs `[build] dev`, `cargo build --locked`, leaving the rung's debug
  binary at `target/debug/vc-x1`. After a validation it reuses the test build, so it costs under a
  second, and `vc-x1 run-dev` runs it first, so what runs is always the current code.
- Release: `vc-x1 build` runs `[build] release`, `cargo build --release --locked`, leaving the
  release build at `target/release/vc-x1` with a stamp beside it naming the commit it was built
  from ([build](#build)).
- Install: at a cycle's Land, `vc-x1 install` runs the release build, which cargo skips when
  nothing changed, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin`, the `[install] dir`, after reporting what it
  is copying ([install](#install)). It is the one command that touches the PATH.

Where each build leaves its binary is the config's to say, `[build] release-bin` and `dev-bin`:
vc-x1 never works it out from cargo or the package's name.

The commands in the order a cycle uses them, a rung's loop first and Land after:

| Command | What it does | When |
|---|---|---|
| `vc-x1 validate` | fmt, clippy, every test | every rung, before review |
| `vc-x1 validate --fast` | the unit tests only | while iterating |
| `vc-x1 build-dev` | the dev build, into `target/debug` | to build without running |
| `vc-x1 run-dev` | `build-dev`, then runs it | trying the change |
| `vc-x1 build` | the release, into `target/release`, with its stamp | at Land, or to try the release profile |
| `vc-x1 run` | `build`, then runs it | the smoke check before install |
| `vc-x1 install` | `build`, then reports it and copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` | at Land |

`validate` checks the source and makes no build of either kind. `run`, `run-dev`, and `install`
------

### build

Build the workspace's release with `build`, or its dev build with `build-dev`, by the work side's
`[build]` table (see [Workspace config tables](#workspace-config-tables)). The lists run as
[validate](#validate)'s do: each element one command, split on whitespace with no shell in between,

  `dirty` when `@` held edits that were compiled too, and the binary's size and modification

Build the release if it is out of date, then copy it into the install directory, the one command
that touches the PATH, at a cycle's Land. It first runs `[build] release` exactly as
[build](#build) does, the stamp included. Cargo rebuilds only what changed, so with nothing changed

refused. It then copies `[build] release-bin`, `target/release/vc-x1` here, into the one directory

directory being on it is what puts the copy on the PATH. `~` in the directory expands against your
home, so the committed value fits every machine. The copy is a temporary file renamed into place,
so a running copy of the old binary is undisturbed and a failed copy leaves it as it was.

- the version, noting a suffixed (pre-release) one and a manifest version that differs
- the commit, and whether it is `main` and `main@origin`
- the state, `clean`, `dirty`, or `unknown`

  `vc-x1 build` is named

not run, or a missing install directory.

I don't think `--root`, or the lack of it, is what did this. Here's what's on disk:

- **`~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1`:** written at 08:26:35 today. It reports `0.85.7-3+ba76874d23d7`, clean, which is the install rung commit just pushed.
- **`target/release/vc-x1`:** rebuilt at 08:31:56 by my `install --dry-run`, which copied nothing ("[dry-run] copied nothing").
- **`[build]` and `[validate]`:** neither list writes outside `target/`. Plain `cargo build --release --locked` never touches `~/.cargo/bin`.

So the 08:26 copy came from something that copies onto the PATH: a real `vc-x1 install`, or a hand `cargo install`. I didn't run either. Did you run `vc-x1 install` after the push?

If so, the cause is `install` itself. It copies whatever release build it's given, suffixed versions included. That was the rule set at the install rung: it reports, and the release process decides. `--root` wouldn't change that, because it only moved where the build landed. Renaming to `vc-x1-dev` would, because the plain name could then never hold a cycle's build.

I see two ways to keep the PATH's `vc-x1` stable:

1. **Use `run-dev` to try a cycle's build (my recommendation, it's already planned):** `vc-x1 run-dev <args>` runs `target/debug/vc-x1` without installing anything. That's the run rung's whole purpose. I'd move it up to run next, ahead of the `.gitignore` rung, so trying a change never needs `install`. Optionally, `install` could also refuse a suffixed version unless `--force` is given. That's a narrow reversal of "refuses nothing", for the one case that clearly matters to us.
2. **Rename to `vc-x1-dev` while a cycle runs:** this works, but it brings back the rename and Land-restore steps this cycle deliberately skipped. It also only protects the name, while `install` would still copy anything it's given.

Either way, the binary on your PATH right now is a dev build, `0.85.7-3`. Getting back to the last landed version means building from `main` (`d70cf9ec`) and installing that. I'll leave that until you say.

The plain version: your build commands never touch `~/.cargo/bin`; only `install`, or a hand `cargo install`, does. The planned `run-dev` lets you try the dev build without installing it, and `install` could refuse a pre-release version so this can't happen by accident.

Which way do you want to go, and should `install` refuse a suffixed version?

content.text:
That makes sense. Testing `install` means running it, and running it copies onto the real PATH, because `[install] dir` points at `~/.cargo/bin`. `--root` was never in play: it only decided where the build landed, not where `install` copies to.

Three ways to test `install` without replacing your `vc-x1`:

1. **`--dir <DIR>` on `install` (my recommendation):** it overrides `[install] dir` for one run, so a test is `cargo run -- install --dir tmp/bin`. That exercises everything for real: the build, the report, and the copy that renames into place. Nothing on the PATH changes. It's small, a flag plus one test, and works the same for any project using vc-x1. `--dry-run` stays for when you only want the report.
2. **Rename to `vc-x1-dev` for the cycle:** this is the agent-files' own rule, Opening step 6, which this cycle bent. With it, testing `install` puts `vc-x1-dev` next to `vc-x1`, which is exactly the rule's purpose. But doing it mid-cycle reaches the package's binary name, `release-bin`/`dev-bin`, and whatever the tests and docs call the binary, and Land has to restore it all. That's a lot of change to make in the middle of a cycle.
3. **Testing through `HOME`:** `HOME=tmp/h vc-x1 install` works today with no code change, since `~` expands against `HOME`. But it's easy to forget, and it changes what everything else in that run sees.

My recommendation is option 1. It could go into this stamp rung, but it's a different subject. I'd make it a small inserted rung right after this one, `feat: install takes --dir`, ahead of the `.gitignore` rung.

Your PATH currently has the dev `0.85.7-3` from your test. When we're done, getting the landed version back means building `main` (`d70cf9ec`) and installing that, or installing at this cycle's Land.

The plain version: `install` always copies to your real bin directory, so testing it replaces your working `vc-x1`. A `--dir` flag lets a test copy somewhere harmless instead.

message.content: Having --dir is necessary, but we might want `install-dev` mirroring `build-dev` and `run-dev` too?

content.text:
Yes, I think it's worth having, and it covers something `run-dev` can't.

**What it would do:** `install-dev` runs `build-dev`, then copies `[build] dev-bin` into `[install] dir` under the name with `-dev` appended, here `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1-dev`. It uses the same report and the same copy that renames into place as `install`. `vc-x1` stays the landed release, and `vc-x1-dev` is the cycle's build, side by side on the PATH. That's what renaming the package to `vc-x1-dev` was for, but it happens at the copy, so nothing gets renamed and Land has nothing to restore.

**Why `run-dev` isn't enough:** `run-dev` finds its binary through the config of the workspace you're standing in. Run from iiac-perf, it runs iiac-perf's dev build, not vc-x1's. So the only way to try a cycle's vc-x1 against another project is a dev binary on the PATH under its own name. `install-dev` gives you that.

**The name fits now:** at the build rung we dropped "install-dev" because it named a build that never reached the PATH. This one does reach it, so `install`/`install-dev` pairs up with `build`/`build-dev` and `run`/`run-dev`, the `-dev` suffix meaning the dev build in all three.

**`--dir` is still needed:** `install-dev` exercises the copy, but not the release path. Testing `install` itself still needs `--dir`, and `install-dev` would take it too.

**Questions for you:**
- **The name:** always `<dev-bin's file name>-dev`, or a config key such as `[install] dev-name`? I'd go with the fixed suffix: one rule, nothing to configure, and a project wanting another name can add a key later.
- **Where:** I'd make it its own rung right after `--dir`, since it reuses `--dir` and the copy code. The order would be stamp, `--dir`, `install-dev`, `.gitignore`, run, closing. It could also fold into the `--dir` rung, but that rung would then be about two things.

One thing to keep in mind: `vc-x1-dev` is a debug build, three to five times slower, which is fine for trying a change.

The plain version: `install-dev` puts this cycle's build on your PATH as `vc-x1-dev`, next to your normal `vc-x1`, so you can try it in any project without replacing anything.

Do you want it as its own rung after `--dir`, named with the fixed `-dev` suffix?

# Process-spawn ban, since 0.79.0. The mechanism, the ban as config,
# the grant as an attribute, this comment as the register, is
# explained in README.md under "No process spawns". A new
# `Command::new` site needs an entry below and a visible
# `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` naming it.
#
# The register, closed (wink, 2026-08-19), reopened for entries 5,
# 6, and 7:
#
# 1. Version gate: the `jj -V` probe (src/version.rs). The gate
#    exists to compare the user's jj CLI against our jj-lib, so the
#    CLI spawn is its subject matter.
# 2. Closed 2026-10-20 by the "feat: vc-x1 commit, install, and
#    run-dev" cycle: push's `$EDITOR` launch (src/push.rs) went with
#    push's message stage, since `commit` carries the description
#    and push publishes what was reviewed. The number stays so the
#    later entries keep theirs.
# 3. Init's gh provisioning (src/init.rs): `gh auth status`,
#    `gh repo view`, `gh repo create`. Creating a repo on GitHub is
#    the forge's REST API, not a version-control operation, and no jj or
#    git library can do it, and gh is GitHub's authenticated client.
# 4. Test helpers (src/test_helpers.rs and tests/common/mod.rs):
#    real-jj/git fixture setup and interop verification, kept
#    deliberately independent of the facade under test, and never a
#    substitute for asserting our jj-lib paths directly. The CLI
#    tests' launcher spawning the built vc-x1 binary is this entry
#    too: spawning the binary is what a CLI test is.
# 5. A configured command list (src/command_list.rs): runs the
#    workspace's `[validate]` commands for validate and its
#    `[build]` commands for build and build-dev, which is each
#    command's whole job. Opened 2026-08-21 by the "empty
#    custom-family into the pinned set and config" cycle, whose plan
#    put the checklist commands in config for one subcommand to run,
#    and widened to the build lists by "feat: vc-x1 install stages,
#    deploys, and runs builds", the one site moved out of
#    src/validate.rs so all three share it.
# 6. Sync's remote look (src/jj/session.rs, `git_command`): two
#    git commands that ask a remote and move no ref. `git ls-remote
#    --heads <remote>` gives the commit each of the remote's
#    bookmarks is on, and `git fetch --refmap= --no-tags
#    --no-write-fetch-head` downloads the commits of the ones that
#    moved, so a fast-forward can be told from a rewrite before
#    anything is fetched. Sync has to know what a fetch would do
#    before it makes one, and a fetch changes the repo. jj-lib has no
#    such query: it spawns git itself for its network legs and keeps
#    that layer private, and it builds gix with no network client,
#    as of 0.45.1 and 0.46.0. Opened 2026-10-09 (wink) by the
#    "feat: sync is safe by default" cycle, and temporary: the entry
#    closes when jj-lib offers the query (TODO.md > ## Waiting).
# 7. The workspace's release build (src/install_cmd.rs): install
#    runs the binary it is about to copy, `-V` alone, to report the
#    version and commit it shows beside the manifest. Opened
#    2026-10-21 by "feat: vc-x1 install stages, deploys, and runs
#    builds", whose run rung runs the same artifacts.
#
# jj-lib's own git children (fetch/push/clone network legs, the
# default-branch query) are jj-lib's implementation detail, not
# vc-x1 spawn sites, and no lint here sees them.
#
# Environment-write ban, since 0.84.35 (bug 21 in notes/bugs.md).
# Tests run as threads of one process, so a write to its environment
# is seen by every test running beside it: `HOME` set to `/h` by one
# test had git look for the signing key under `/h` in another, and
# the jj children the sync tests spawn find no config. A new
# `set_var` / `remove_var` site needs an entry below and a visible
# `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` naming it.
#
# The register:
#
# 1. `init::tests::expand_vars_envvar` (src/init/tests.rs): sets
#    and removes `VC_X1_TEST_EXPAND_VAR`, which no other test reads.
# 2. `keep_env_preserves_fixture_across_drop` (tests/cli_keep.rs):
#    sets and removes `VC_X1_TEST_KEEP`, the only test in its own
#    test binary, so no other test shares its process.
disallowed-methods = [
    { path = "std::process::Command::new", reason = "vc-x1 runs jj and git through jj-lib and gix, never by spawning their binaries: a new spawn site needs an entry in the register comment at the top of clippy.toml and a visible #[allow] at the site (README: No process spawns)" },
    { path = "std::env::set_var", reason = "a write to the process environment is seen by every test running beside it (bug 21): pass the value in instead, or add an entry to the environment-write register in clippy.toml and a visible #[allow] at the site" },
    { path = "std::env::remove_var", reason = "a write to the process environment is seen by every test running beside it (bug 21): pass the value in instead, or add an entry to the environment-write register in clippy.toml and a visible #[allow] at the site" },
]
