- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

3	Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as

7	## A work rung
8	
9	Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`
10	
11	```
12	Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
13	config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
14	disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.
15	
16	* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
17	  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
18	    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
19	    stops there.
20	  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
21	    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
22	* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
23	  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
24	    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
25	    the file's shape.
26	```
27	
28	The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
29	is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
30	diff already lists.

132:### Commit-body form
133-
134-The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
135-shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
136-problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
137-bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
138-statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
139-
140-- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
141-  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
142-  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
143-  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
144-  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
145-- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
146-  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
147-  to be more than one commit.
148-- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
149-  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
150-  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
151-- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
152-  form, the general form at its smallest.
153-- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
154-  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
155-  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.

157-**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the

feat: vc-x1 install copies the release build

Land's promotion is a hand-typed cargo install, which checks nothing
and builds a fresh binary rather than copying the one tested, and the
builds run through cargo install --root, one dropped flag from
replacing the binary on the PATH.

Solution: vc-x1 install runs the release build as vc-x1 build does, a
no-op when nothing changed, reports the binary's version, its commit
against main and main@origin, its state, and whether its stamp still
matches, and copies it into the install directory as a temporary file
renamed into place, refusing only a copy that would be wrong. The
builds become plain cargo build into target/, build says whether the
binary was built or up to date, the binary's -V is read at its first
version line, and the Todo gains three entries. See details in
zCLOSED.md.

ochid: /.claude/tytvyonsnqrr

-----
feat: status takes the write commands' scope

Status parsed its scope on its own, long names, a positional, and comma
forms, while the write commands took w, a, b, and p through a bare
function that gave tab completion nothing to offer.

Solution: one builder makes each command's -s parser from the scopes it
offers, so status takes the write commands' four and every -s completes
exactly what its command takes, a scope it does not offer still parsing
to reach the command's own refusal. Status's positional and comma forms
are gone, a plain repo is -s p, and the Todo gains an entry for shell
completion asking the binary typed. See details in zCLOSED.md.

Title: `feat: the release stamp goes, cargo tracks staleness`

Body (in `tmp/stamp-body.txt`):

```
The release build wrote a stamp beside its binary, a record of the
commit and state it was built from, so build could say the binary was
up to date and install could say whether it still matched. That made
vc-x1 a second judge of staleness beside cargo, one that could disagree
with it and that read a file a failed or skipped build could leave
behind.

Solution: the stamp is gone, cargo alone decides what to rebuild, and
vc-x1 runs the configured build list and checks its result, a release
that passes but leaves no binary at build.release-bin being an error.
Build logs the binary with the commit and state of the workspace, and
install reports what the binary's -V shows, a binary reporting no
commit being reported as unknown rather than guessed. The cycle record
also loses a duplicated block an earlier edit introduced. See details
in zCLOSED.md.
```

May I commit and push?

##### feat: vc-x1 build stages the release

The release is built under its own root with a stamp naming the commit it came from, so it can be
run before anything on the PATH is replaced, and `build-dev` is the dev build on demand.

- `vc-x1 build` runs `[build] release`, now `--root tmp/rel`, and writes the stamp beside the new
  `[build] release-bin`, recording the commit, the state of the source code that was compiled,
  and the binary's size and modification time. The old stamp is removed before the build and the
  new one written only once it passes and the binary is there, so no stamp outlives a failed
  build.
- `vc-x1 build-dev` runs `[build] dev` and writes no stamp.
- Both builds' commands, and `validate`'s, get the commit and the state in their environment, and
  vc-x1 compiles them in, so its banner carries the commit as build metadata and `vc-x1 version`
  a `build` line, wherever the binary is copied.
- `build.rs` falls back to git's `HEAD` when no variables are passed, so a hand-typed cargo build
  reports its commit too, marked `.unknown`. The `HEAD` reader is its own file, compiled by
  `build.rs` and by the crate's tests.
- The names: the rung began as `install` with `--dev`, the dev build became `install-dev`, and
  both became `build` and `build-dev`, `install` kept for the step onto the PATH. The table is
  `[build]`, its keys the ones the last cycle landed under `[install]`.
- `[validate] full` no longer builds the dev binary, which `run-dev` will build first.
- Running a configured command list moved out of `validate` into a module the three share, so the
  one spawn site serves them, and clippy's register entry 5 is widened to say so.
- Status takes `w`, `a`, and `b` for its scope, hidden aliases of the long names, the stopgap for
  **status takes the write commands' scope**.
- The schema's `install.*` keys become `build.*`, with `build.release-bin` new and the release
  reworded as the staged build, and the model is regenerated. The README's build section
  describes the stages and the commands in a cycle's order, gains a `build` section, and lists
  `[build]` among the config tables.

##### feat: status takes the write commands' scope

Status's `-s` takes the same four scopes as every write command, so one parser serves them all,
and status's own positional and comma forms go.

- Status's `-s` takes `w|work`, `a|agent`, `b|both`, and `p|por`, absent `work`.
- Every `-s` taking a `RepoScope`, status's and the eight write commands', is a parser made by one
  builder from the scopes the command offers: the long names declared for completion, the short
  ones as hidden aliases, the scopes not offered and `bot` declared hidden so they still reach the
  command's refusal or the fix-it, and the value handed to `parse_repo_scope`.
- `p` reports the repo `-R` names or the cwd's as itself, labeled `por`, resolved by the write
  commands' resolver, so it is refused on a side of a workspace with the same error they give.
- The positional scope, `status both`, and the comma forms `work,agent` and `agent,work` are
  gone, and status's old keyword parser with them, the stopgap aliases included.
- The README's status section and synopsis describe the four scopes, and its examples use `-s`.

##### feat: vc-x1 install copies the release build

The release build, the one tested, is copied to where consumers run it, after a report of what it
is, for the user and the release process to judge.

- `vc-x1 install` copies `[build] release-bin` into the new `[install] dir`, `~` expanded, as a
  temporary file beside the destination renamed into place, the file name kept. `$PATH` is not
  searched.
- It runs the release build first through `build`'s own code, the stamp included, a no-op for
  cargo when nothing changed, and checks `[install] dir` before it, so a workspace with nothing
  to install builds nothing.
- `build` says whether the release binary was `built` or `up to date`, from its size and time
  before and after the list, so a no-op build shows that the binary tested is the one copied.
- It then gathers the facts, `main`, `main@origin`, the manifest's version, the stamp, the
  binary's size and time, and what its `-V` reports, and reports the version, the commit placed
  against `main` and `main@origin`, the state, and whether the stamp matches the binary, and
  refuses only a missing binary, a `-V` that will not run, or a missing install directory, listing
  every reason. `--dry-run` builds and reports, and copies nothing.
- Running the binary's `-V` is clippy's spawn register entry 7. Its output is read at the first
  line whose second word starts with a digit, so a line printed before the version is passed
  over, and output with no such line is unreadable and refused, found when wink's test
  `println!` ahead of the banner was read as the version `hi` and copied.
- `[build]` becomes plain `cargo build`, `--release --locked` and `--locked`, the binaries in
  `target/release` and `target/debug`, and "staged" leaves the help, the docs, and the messages.
- Every `unwrap_or*` the cycle added carries its `// OK:` comment, five of them in this rung and
  three the build rung pushed without one, `build_env`'s and two in the banner's state, a miss
  caught here.
- The schema gains `install.dir`, the build keys' examples follow the new lists, the model is
  regenerated, and the README's overview, `build` section, and config tables follow, with a new
  `install` section.
- Three Todo entries arrive with the rung's review: **Every repo's .gitignore ignores .claude, and
  settings stay out of agent-repos**, to run as the next rung, **A config file says what and its
  constraints, and the why is in the cycle record**, and **The release stamp is reconsidered now
  that install builds**.

  `[build]`, its keys the ones the last cycle landed under `[install]`.

  one spawn site serves them, and clippy's register entry 5 is widened to say so.

  **status takes the write commands' scope**.

  reworded as the staged build, and the model is regenerated. The README's build section

##### feat: status takes the write commands' scope

Status's `-s` takes the same four scopes as every write command, so one parser serves them all,
and status's own positional and comma forms go.

- Status's `-s` takes `w|work`, `a|agent`, `b|both`, and `p|por`, absent `work`.
- Every `-s` taking a `RepoScope`, status's and the eight write commands', is a parser made by one
  builder from the scopes the command offers: the long names declared for completion, the short
  ones as hidden aliases, the scopes not offered and `bot` declared hidden so they still reach the
  command's refusal or the fix-it, and the value handed to `parse_repo_scope`.
- `p` reports the repo `-R` names or the cwd's as itself, labeled `por`, resolved by the write
  commands' resolver, so it is refused on a side of a workspace with the same error they give.

  gone, and status's old keyword parser with them, the stopgap aliases included.

is, for the user and the release process to judge.

  searched.

  before and after the list, so a no-op build shows that the binary tested is the one copied.

  binary's size and time, and what its `-V` reports, and reports the version, the commit placed

  refuses only a missing binary, a `-V` that will not run, or a missing install directory, listing
  every reason. `--dry-run` builds and reports, and copies nothing.

  line whose second word starts with a digit, so a line printed before the version is passed
  over, and output with no such line is unreadable and refused, found when wink's test

    /// Build the release if out of date, then copy it into the install directory
    #[command(
        long_about = "Build the release if out of date, then copy it into the install directory.\n\n\
        It first runs `[build] release`, exactly as `vc-x1 build` does.\n\
        Cargo rebuilds only what changed, so with nothing changed\n\
        the binary already tested is the one copied. The build leaves the\n\
        release at `[build] release-bin` (here `target/release/vc-x1`), and\n\
        `install` copies it into the one directory `[install] dir` names\n\
        (here `~/.cargo/bin`, `~` expanded), under the same file name. It\n\
        does not search $PATH. The copy goes to a temporary file renamed into\n\
        place, so a running copy of the old binary is undisturbed and a\n\
        failed copy leaves the old one.\n\n\
        Before copying it reports what it is copying: the version and commit\n\
        the binary's -V shows, whether that commit is `main` and\n\
        `main@origin`, clean or dirty, and a version with a cycle's suffix.\n\
        A binary whose -V carries no commit is reported as unknown. The\n\
        report is for you to judge, and refuses nothing: which builds may be\n\
        installed is the release process's call, not the tool's. It refuses\n\
        only when the copy itself would be wrong: no binary at `release-bin`\n\
        after the build, a binary whose -V will not run, or a missing install\n\
        directory. --dry-run builds and reports, and copies nothing. A\n\
        workspace with no `[install] dir` has nothing to install, and builds\n\
        nothing."
    )]
    Install(install_cmd::InstallArgs),
| `-R, --repo <DIR>` | Workspace to build from, for both commands [default: the one containing the current directory] |

### install

Build the release if it is out of date, then copy it into the install directory, the one command
that touches the PATH, at a cycle's Land. It first runs `[build] release` exactly as
[build](#build) does. Cargo rebuilds only what changed, so with nothing changed
the binary already tested is the one copied, and a missing or stale one is built rather than
refused. It then copies `[build] release-bin`, `target/release/vc-x1` here, into the one directory
`[install] dir` names, `~/.cargo/bin` here, under the same file name. `$PATH` is not searched: the
directory being on it is what puts the copy on the PATH. `~` in the directory expands against your
home, so the committed value fits every machine. The copy is a temporary file renamed into place,
so a running copy of the old binary is undisturbed and a failed copy leaves it as it was.

It first reports what it is copying, from the binary's own `-V`:

- the version, noting a suffixed (pre-release) one and a manifest version that differs
- the commit, and whether it is `main` and `main@origin`
- the state, `clean`, `dirty`, or `unknown`

A binary whose `-V` carries no commit, another project's that does not compile the build
variables in, is reported as `commit unknown` and `state unknown`.

The report refuses nothing. Which builds may be installed is the release process's call, not the
tool's: here a cycle's Land runs `install` on `main` after the push, and a project releasing from
a branch or a tag makes it differently. `install` refuses only when the copy itself would be
wrong, listing every reason: no binary at `release-bin` after the build, a binary whose `-V` will
not run, or a missing install directory.

`--dry-run` builds and reports, and copies nothing. A workspace with no `[install] dir` has
nothing to install, and `install` says so before building anything.

```
# At Land, on main after the push: build and smoke-test, then install, its build a no-op
vc-x1 build
target/release/vc-x1 -V
vc-x1 install
```

The report, run on a cycle's bookmark with edits in `@`:

```
install: '/home/me/proj/target/release/vc-x1' -> '/home/me/.cargo/bin/vc-x1'
install:   version 0.85.7-3, a suffixed (pre-release) version
install:   commit 38a446f041da, not `main`
install:   state dirty
install: [dry-run] copied nothing
```

The build's own lines, `build: [1/1] cargo build --release --locked` and the rest, come first.

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `--dry-run` | Build and report, and copy nothing |
| `-R, --repo <DIR>` | Workspace to install from [default: the one containing the current directory] |

### install

Build the release if it is out of date, then copy it into the install directory, the one command
that touches the PATH, at a cycle's Land. It first runs `[build] release` exactly as
[build](#build) does. Cargo rebuilds only what changed, so with nothing changed
the binary already tested is the one copied, and a missing or stale one is built rather than
refused. It then copies `[build] release-bin`, `target/release/vc-x1` here, into the one directory
`[install] dir` names, `~/.cargo/bin` here, under the same file name. `$PATH` is not searched: the
directory being on it is what puts the copy on the PATH. `~` in the directory expands against your
home, so the committed value fits every machine. The copy is a temporary file renamed into place,
so a running copy of the old binary is undisturbed and a failed copy leaves it as it was.

It first reports what it is copying, from the binary's own `-V`:

- the version, noting a suffixed (pre-release) one and a manifest version that differs
- the commit, and whether it is `main` and `main@origin`
- the state, `clean`, `dirty`, or `unknown`

A binary whose `-V` carries no commit, another project's that does not compile the build
variables in, is reported as `commit unknown` and `state unknown`.

The report refuses nothing. Which builds may be installed is the release process's call, not the
tool's: here a cycle's Land runs `install` on `main` after the push, and a project releasing from
a branch or a tag makes it differently. `install` refuses only when the copy itself would be
wrong, listing every reason: no binary at `release-bin` after the build, a binary whose `-V` will
not run, or a missing install directory.

`--dry-run` builds and reports, and copies nothing. A workspace with no `[install] dir` has
nothing to install, and `install` says so before building anything.

```
# At Land, on main after the push: build and smoke-test, then install, its build a no-op
vc-x1 build
target/release/vc-x1 -V
vc-x1 install
```

```

install:   version 0.85.7-3, a suffixed (pre-release) version
install:   commit 38a446f041da, not `main`
install:   state dirty
install: [dry-run] copied nothing
```

The build's own lines, `build: [1/1] cargo build --release --locked` and the rest, come first.

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `--dry-run` | Build and report, and copy nothing |
| `-R, --repo <DIR>` | Workspace to install from [default: the one containing the current directory] |

The `--dir` rung is done, at 0.85.7-5, in the uncommitted `@`. Full validation passed: 11 suites, 0 failed. The anchors check clean.

- **The flag:** `vc-x1 install --dir <DIR>` copies into `DIR` instead of `[install] dir` for that run.
  - The config key isn't needed when you pass `--dir`.
  - The error for a missing directory now says "the install directory" instead of naming the config key, since the flag may have named it.
- **Relative paths, my call:** a relative `--dir` counts from the current directory, like any path argument. `[install] dir` counts from the config file's directory. `--dir` doesn't expand `~` itself; the shell already does.
- **Tested for real:** I ran `cargo run --locked -- install --dir tmp/bin`. The release copy went into `tmp/bin` and reports `0.85.7-5+a2f326dbbc8f.dirty`. `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1` kept its 08:26:35 time.

- **Tests:** `flags_parse` covers `--dir`. A new test, `dir_overrides_the_install_dir`, checks that `--dir` wins and that no `[install] dir` is needed with it.
  - The test's first version failed because resolving the release build needs a jj repo.
  - So the directory choice is now its own small function, `dest_dir`, and the test checks that.
- **Docs:** the install help, the README install section (with a `tmp/bin` test example and an options-table row), and the rung's subsection in `zDOING.md`.

No new `unwrap`/`expect`/`unwrap_or*` outside tests.

6:- [Build and install](#build-and-install)
## Build and install

A plain Rust crate: `cargo build` and `cargo test` of one binary, `vc-x1`, named by the
manifest's `[package].name`, which never changes. The `[build]` table in `.vc-config.md` holds two
builds, each a plain `cargo build` leaving its binary in `target/`, off the PATH, so nothing a
cycle builds replaces the `vc-x1` on the PATH until the cycle lands. Both are `--locked`, so they
compile the same dependencies, the ones `Cargo.lock` commits:

- Dev: `vc-x1 build-dev` runs `[build] dev`, `cargo build --locked`, leaving the rung's debug
  binary at `target/debug/vc-x1`. After a validation it reuses the test build, so it costs under a
  second, and `vc-x1 run-dev` runs it first, so what runs is always the current code.
- Release: `vc-x1 build` runs `[build] release`, `cargo build --release --locked`, leaving the
  release build at `target/release/vc-x1`, its `-V` naming the commit it was built from
  ([build](#build)).
- Install: at a cycle's Land, `vc-x1 install` runs the release build, which cargo skips when
  nothing changed, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin`, the `[install] dir`, after reporting what it
  is copying ([install](#install)). It is the one command that touches the PATH.

Where each build leaves its binary is the config's to say, `[build] release-bin` and `dev-bin`:
vc-x1 never works it out from cargo or the package's name.

The commands in the order a cycle uses them, a rung's loop first and Land after:

| Command | What it does | When |
|---|---|---|
| `vc-x1 validate` | fmt, clippy, every test | every rung, before review |
| `vc-x1 validate --fast` | the unit tests only | while iterating |
| `vc-x1 build-dev` | the dev build, into `target/debug` | to build without running |
| `vc-x1 run-dev` | `build-dev`, then runs it | trying the change |
| `vc-x1 build` | the release, into `target/release` | at Land, or to try the release profile |
| `vc-x1 run` | `build`, then runs it | the smoke check before install |
| `vc-x1 install` | `build`, then reports it and copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` | at Land |

`validate` checks the source and makes no build of either kind. `run`, `run-dev`, and `install`
build first, as `cargo run` does, and cargo rebuilds only what changed, so the binary `run`
smoke-tests is the one `install` copies.

- `target/debug/vc-x1 -V` names the exact rung, since the version-of-record carries the cycle's

message.content: How is [build].release-bin and dev-bin used, those are defaults from cargo builds I think

content.text: How is [build].release-bin and dev-bin used, those are defaults from cargo builds I think

Yes. Those values are where cargo puts this package's binary by default: `target/<profile>/<bin name>`, with `release` for `--release` and `debug` otherwise. They're written in the config instead of worked out, because `[build] release` and `dev` are arbitrary command lists. vc-x1 can't know where a list leaves its binary. A different target directory (`CARGO_TARGET_DIR`), a `--target <triple>` build (`target/<triple>/release/`), a renamed `[[bin]]`, or a non-cargo build would each put it somewhere else. So the config says where, and vc-x1 checks that it's there.

How each one is used:

- **`release-bin`:**
  - `build`: checks the file is there after the list passes. A pass that leaves nothing there is an error naming the key.
  - `install`: runs its `-V` for the report, then copies it into `[install] dir` (or `--dir`) under its own name.
  - `run` (the run rung, still to come): will run it.
- **`dev-bin`:**
  - `install-dev` (this rung): runs its `-V` for the report, then copies it as `<name>-dev`. A missing file after the build is a refusal naming `build.dev-bin`.
  - `run-dev` (the run rung): will run it.
  - `build-dev` doesn't check it. Only the release build checks its binary. It could check too, for symmetry, but I left `build-dev` as it was.

The plain version: yes, they're cargo's default output paths. They're in the config so a project that builds differently can say where its binary ends up.

content.text:
That's a fair point, and the symmetry is cheap to have. My proposal, mirroring `[build]`:

```toml
[build]
release-bin = "target/release/vc-x1"
dev-bin = "target/debug/vc-x1"

[install]
release-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
dev-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
```

- **Rename `dir` to `release-dir`:** it pairs with `release-bin` the way `dev-dir` pairs with `dev-bin`. `dir` arrived in this cycle's install rung and hasn't landed, so nothing outside the cycle uses it yet.
- **Each command reads its own key:** `install` reads `release-dir` and `install-dev` reads `dev-dir`. `--dir` overrides whichever one the command reads, for one run.
- **No fallback:** a missing `dev-dir` means `install-dev` has nothing to install. It says so before building, as `install` does now. The bin keys are explicit in the same way.
- **The `-dev` suffix stays:** both keys can name the same directory, as they do here, and the suffix is what keeps the dev build from overwriting the release there. A project that sets `dev-dir` to, say, `tmp/bin` still gets `tmp/bin/vc-x1-dev`.

This widens the rung beyond what we agreed, so I'm stopping to ask. Should I make these changes in this rung, with the rename and the suffix as above? Or do you want different names, or no suffix when the directories differ?

content.text:
By "scriptable" I take it you mean that, like `[build] release` and `dev`, installing becomes a configured command list instead of vc-x1's built-in copy. Two facts about how lists run today shape that (`src/command_list.rs:14-19`):

- **No shell:** each element is split on whitespace into a program and its arguments. A command can't expand `~` or `$VAR`, or use quotes, unless it is `sh <script file>`.
- **Environment variables:** a caller can add variables to every command in the list. That is how `build` passes `VC_X1_BUILD_COMMIT`.

So a scripted install could look like this:

```toml
[install]
release-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
dev-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
release = ["sh scripts/install.sh"]   # optional: replaces the built-in copy

# vc-config: settable configuration keys

This file is two things at once, and that is the point: the **schema prototype** vc-x1 is built
from, and the **long-form documentation** every generated `reference:` url lands on. One `##`
section per settable key holds that key's prose and, in a `toml` fence, that key's metadata, so
the documentation and the schema cannot describe different keys.

It is not a config file. Your workspace's config is `.vc-config.md` (note the leading dot).
Editing this file changes what the binary knows, takes effect on the next build, and is reviewed
like any source change.

## How this file is read

The format is the config markdown carrier's own: the `toml` fences, concatenated in document
order, form the TOML that gets parsed. build.rs shares the filter (`src/md_fence.rs`) with the
instance-config loader, so the prototype and a `.vc-config.md` are read by one rule, and prose
outside the fences never reaches a parser.

The tag must be exactly `toml`. A fence tagged anything else, or tagged not at all, is prose like
the text around it and never reaches the parser, which is what lets one of these files show a
specimen config in a `text` fence without the specimen becoming configuration.

Shape: one TOML table per settable key, named by the key's path, dynamic segments quoted
(`[repo.category."<cat>"]`). Key order here is rendering order everywhere downstream. The
entries a key's table may carry:

- `homes`: which config file(s) may contain the key. vc-x1 writes it only into those files, and
  `vc-x1 config --validate` reports it as unknown anywhere else. The values:
  - `"user"`: the user-wide config, `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` (or
    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vc-x1/config.toml`). One per user, still TOML rather than markdown
  - `"workspace-code"`, `"workspace-agent"`: the work side's and the agent side's instance config
- `kind`: value shape, one of `"str"`, `"usize"`, `"bool"`, `"item-list"` (a comma-separated
  list in one string), `"str-list"` (a TOML array of strings, one element per item)
- `doc`: one-line description (rendered into generated configs, so keep it tight)
- `used-by`: what reads the value once it is set, which is a different question from `homes`:
  the command or flag it feeds, or the structural role it plays
- `default`: the built-in value, omitted when there is none
- `example`: representative value for keys with no default
- `required`: active (not commented) in generated configs. The value is role-specific, filled by
  `init`
- `reference`: optional override url for the key's docs. When absent (the norm) build.rs derives
  `<reference-base>/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<anchor of the path>`, which is the key's own section
  below

## The prototype's own metadata

`[vc-config]` is this file's metadata rather than a settable key. `reference-base` is the bare
repo url every derived reference is built from: build.rs joins it with `/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#`
and the key's heading anchor, so a reference follows the repo's default branch and no branch name
is baked in. A fork points it at its own repo and edits its own copy of this file.

```toml
[vc-config]
reference-base = "https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1"
```

## How the keys resolve

The `agent-session.*` keys resolve git-style, most specific wins: CLI flag, then the workspace
instance config, then the user config (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`), then the built-in default.

long_about = "Build the release if out of date, then copy it into the install directory.\n\n\
        It first runs `[build] release`, exactly as `vc-x1 build` does.\n\
        Cargo rebuilds only what changed, so with nothing changed\n\
        the binary already tested is the one copied. The build leaves the\n\
        release at `[build] release-bin` (here `target/release/vc-x1`), and\n\
        `install` copies it into the one directory `[install] dir` names\n\
        (here `~/.cargo/bin`, `~` expanded), under the same file name. It\n\
        does not search $PATH. The copy goes to a temporary file renamed into\n\
        place, so a running copy of the old binary is undisturbed and a\n\
        failed copy leaves the old one.\n\n\
        Before copying it reports what it is copying: the version and commit\n\
        the binary's -V shows, whether that commit is `main` and\n\
        `main@origin`, clean or dirty, and a version with a cycle's suffix.\n\
        A binary whose -V carries no commit is reported as unknown. The\n\
        report is for you to judge, and refuses nothing: which builds may be\n\
        installed is the release process's call, not the tool's. It refuses\n\
        only when the copy itself would be wrong: no binary at `release-bin`\n\
        after the build, a binary whose -V will not run, or a missing install\n\
        directory. --dry-run builds and reports, and copies nothing.\n\
        --dir DIR copies into DIR instead of `[install] dir` for this run,\n\
        so a test of install leaves the PATH alone, a relative DIR taken\n\
        against the current directory. A workspace with no `[install] dir`\n\
        and no --dir has nothing to install, and builds nothing."
    )]
    Install(install_cmd::InstallArgs),
        long_about = "Build the dev build, then copy it into the install directory as <name>-dev.\n\n\
        It first runs `[build] dev`, exactly as `vc-x1 build-dev` does, then\n\
        copies `[build] dev-bin` (here `target/debug/vc-x1`) into the\n\
        directory `[install] dir` names, or --dir, with `-dev` appended to\n\
        its file name (here `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1-dev`). The landed binary and\n\
        the cycle's dev build then sit side by side on the PATH, so the dev\n\
        build can be tried from any directory, another project's included,\n\
        where `vc-x1 run-dev` would find that project's dev build instead.\n\n\
        The report, the refusals, the copy, --dry-run, and --dir are\n\
        `vc-x1 install`'s, the binary being the dev build's."
    )]
    InstallDev(install_cmd::InstallDevArgs),

Build the release if it is out of date, then copy it into the install directory, the one command
that touches the PATH, at a cycle's Land. It first runs `[build] release` exactly as
[build](#build) does. Cargo rebuilds only what changed, so with nothing changed
the binary already tested is the one copied, and a missing or stale one is built rather than
refused. It then copies `[build] release-bin`, `target/release/vc-x1` here, into the one directory
`[install] dir` names, `~/.cargo/bin` here, under the same file name. `$PATH` is not searched: the
directory being on it is what puts the copy on the PATH. `~` in the directory expands against your
home, so the committed value fits every machine. The copy is a temporary file renamed into place,
so a running copy of the old binary is undisturbed and a failed copy leaves it as it was.

It first reports what it is copying, from the binary's own `-V`:

- the version, noting a suffixed (pre-release) one and a manifest version that differs
- the commit, and whether it is `main` and `main@origin`
- the state, `clean`, `dirty`, or `unknown`

A binary whose `-V` carries no commit, another project's that does not compile the build
variables in, is reported as `commit unknown` and `state unknown`.

The report refuses nothing. Which builds may be installed is the release process's call, not the
tool's: here a cycle's Land runs `install` on `main` after the push, and a project releasing from
a branch or a tag makes it differently. `install` refuses only when the copy itself would be
wrong, listing every reason: no binary at `release-bin` after the build, a binary whose `-V` will
not run, or a missing install directory.

`--dry-run` builds and reports, and copies nothing. `--dir <DIR>` copies into `DIR` instead of
`[install] dir` for the one run, so a test of `install` leaves the PATH alone, a relative `DIR`
taken against the current directory. A workspace with no `[install] dir`, and no `--dir`, has
nothing to install, and `install` says so before building anything.


Build the dev build, then copy it into the install directory with `-dev` appended to its file
name. It first runs `[build] dev` exactly as [build-dev](#build) does, then copies `[build]
dev-bin`, `target/debug/vc-x1` here, into the directory `[install] dir` or `--dir` names, as
`vc-x1-dev`. The landed `vc-x1` and the cycle's `vc-x1-dev` then sit side by side on the PATH, so
the dev build can be tried from any directory, another project's included, where `vc-x1 run-dev`
would run that project's dev build instead. The suffix is fixed: `-dev` always means the dev
build, as in `build-dev` and `run-dev`.

The report, the refusals, the copy, `--dry-run`, and `--dir` are [install](#install)'s, the binary
being the dev build's.

  - Here both are `~/.cargo/bin`, and the `-dev` suffix keeps the two binaries apart.

  - When a list is present, it runs instead of the built-in copy, after the same build, report, and refusals.
  - It gets `VC_X1_INSTALL_BIN`, `VC_X1_INSTALL_DIR` (from the key or `--dir`), and `VC_X1_INSTALL_DEST` in its environment.

  - `command_list` gains `load_optional`: an absent key gives `None`, and a present one is checked as `load` checks it.
  - Clippy's register entry 5 widens to cover the install lists.

  - I put "Optional" at the head of both lists' one-line docs, which the model shows beside them.

message.content: Should build, install, run be symmetrical, seems reasonable?

content.text:
Yes, and most of it is already there. Here is where the three stand:

| | release | dev | config |
|---|---|---|---|
| build | `build` | `build-dev` | `[build] release`, `release-bin`, `dev`, `dev-bin` |
| install | `install` | `install-dev` | `[install] release`, `release-dir`, `dev`, `dev-dir` |
| run (run rung) | `run` | `run-dev` | none yet; it uses `[build]`'s `*-bin` |

- **Already symmetric:** the command pairs, the `-dev` naming, `-R`, and the order "build first, then act on the `*-bin` the build left".
- **Not shared:** `--dir` and `--dry-run` belong to `install` only, since they're about the copy. `run` has nothing to copy.

Full symmetry would add an optional `[run]` table with `release` and `dev` lists that run instead of running the binary directly. That's useful for a wrapper (`valgrind`, an emulator, a remote machine), and it would get `VC_X1_RUN_BIN` like install's variables.
- **The catch:** `run` passes your arguments on to the binary, and a list with no shell has nowhere natural to put them. The options are appending them to the last command, or passing them in an environment variable, and either takes a decision.
- **No second key:** `[run]` needs no `-bin` or `-dir` pair of its own; the binary comes from `[build]`.

My recommendation:
- **Now:** keep the run rung's command shape symmetric, `run` and `run-dev`, each building first and then running its `*-bin`.
- **Later:** add the `[run]` lists when someone needs a wrapper, deciding the argument question then.

That's the same call I made on `dev-dir`, though, and you went for symmetry there. If you want `[run]` in the run rung anyway, I'd append the arguments to the last command of the list.

This only affects the run rung. The `install-dev` rung's review is still open.

content.text:
Right. So the asymmetry is in the flags, not just the config. Taking the two flags one at a time:

- **`--dry-run` fits all three.** For `build`/`build-dev` it would print the list and run nothing. For `run`/`run-dev` it would print what would be run. One wrinkle: `install --dry-run` today does build. It runs the build, reports, and copies nothing, because the report of the binary that would be copied is the point, and that needs the build. So the flag would mean slightly different things:
  - Build, and nothing further: print, run nothing. Their effect is the build itself.
  - Install: build and report, change nothing outside `target/`. The copy is its only effect beyond the build.

  I think that's the honest meaning for each. The alternative, an `install --dry-run` that builds nothing, would report on whatever binary happens to be in `target/`, possibly a stale one.
- **`--dir` belongs to `install` only.** It overrides where the copy goes, and only `install` has a destination. `build`'s output location is decided by its command list, which is cargo here. vc-x1 can't move it without knowing the build tool, which is why `release-bin` is stated, not derived. A `build --dir` would need something like `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, which makes the list cargo-specific.

My recommendation is to add `--dry-run` to `build` and `build-dev` in the run rung, with `run` and `run-dev` getting it there too, so all three pairs take it. `--dir` stays `install`'s. That keeps this rung to `install-dev` and the `[install]` keys.

content.text:
As built, it's both, depending on the config:

- **No list (this workspace):** `install` is `vc-x1 build`, then vc-x1's own copy. It isn't a `cp`. It writes a temporary file beside the destination and renames it into place. That's what lets it replace a binary that's running: a plain `cp target/release/vc-x1 ~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1` onto a `vc-x1` in use fails on Linux with "Text file busy". Before copying, it also gives the report and the refusals.
- **With `[install] release` (or `dev`):** the same build, report, and refusals, then the list runs instead of the copy. That's for a project that installs some other way: a signed copy, a package, another machine.

So `release` and `dev` are in `[install]` like `[build]`'s, but optional. `[build]`'s lists are required, since there's no built-in way to build. `[install]`'s can be left out, because the built-in copy covers the common case.

If the question is whether to keep the lists at all: nothing uses them yet. That's the same situation as `dev-dir`, and you went for symmetry there and asked for install to be scriptable. Without them, `install` is just "build, report, safe copy", and a project that installs differently would wait until someone adds the lists. I'm fine either way. Keeping them costs one optional key per build and about 60 lines with tests.

Nothing is committed yet. Should I keep the lists and commit, or take them out first?

message.content: What is the value of [install].release and dev that is equivalent to the default?

content.text:
There isn't a one-line equivalent. Lists run with no shell, so the three variables can only reach a command through a script:

```toml
[install]
release = ["sh scripts/install.sh"]
release-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
dev = ["sh scripts/install.sh"]
dev-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
```

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# scripts/install.sh: vc-x1's built-in copy, a temporary file renamed into place
set -e
tmp="$VC_X1_INSTALL_DIR/.$(basename "$VC_X1_INSTALL_DEST").vc-x1-install"
cp "$VC_X1_INSTALL_BIN" "$tmp" || { rm -f "$tmp"; exit 1; }
mv "$tmp" "$VC_X1_INSTALL_DEST" || { rm -f "$tmp"; exit 1; }
```

- **One script serves both lists:** `VC_X1_INSTALL_DEST` already carries the `-dev` name for `install-dev`.
- **It's equivalent:** the `mv` is a rename within one directory, so it's atomic and safe over a running binary, like the built-in copy. `cp` keeps the executable bit, minus your umask.

Without a script, the nearest single line has to spell out the paths:

```toml
release = ["install -m 755 target/release/vc-x1 /home/wink/.cargo/bin/vc-x1"]
```

It works over a running binary, because `install(1)` unlinks the old file first. But it isn't equivalent:
- **Not atomic:** the destination is briefly missing.
- **No `~`:** without a shell nothing expands it, so the path is machine-specific.
- **Ignores `--dir`.**

That's worth weighing. Reproducing the default faithfully takes a script file, which says something about how much the lists are worth without a need behind them.

Keep the lists, or take them out before committing?

content.text:
Yes, with one difference in the keys: `[install]`'s are directories. Without the lists:

- **`install`:** run `[build] release`, then copy `[build] release-bin` into `[install] release-dir`, keeping its name (`~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1`).
- **`install-dev`:** run `[build] dev`, then copy `[build] dev-bin` into `[install] dev-dir`, with `-dev` added (`~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1-dev`).

Each also reports the binary from its `-V` and refuses only a copy that would be wrong. `--dir` replaces the directory for one run. The copy is the temporary file renamed into place.

`[install]` would then be just the two directories, `release-dir` and `dev-dir`, paired with `[build]`'s `release-bin` and `dev-bin`.

message.content: it's not obvious, this is exactly the feeling I had this morning of vc-x1 not being a build system, because it gets complicated. You brought of a good point, an install could need signing or many other post build operations, combining with other resources. For vc-x1 that doesn't apply but vc-x1 is a "tool" not just for itself. Which is why the feeling about being a build system. BUT, a significant weakness is that it's "easy" for you to be the tool and do these things but you and I aren't perfect and we make mistakes, which is why we use tools to reduce mistakes.

content.text:
I think there's a line here that answers both of your concerns. vc-x1 shouldn't know how to build, sign, or package anything; that's the project's. Its job is the part where people and agents slip: doing the steps in the right order, on the right binary, and checking each one's result.

`[validate]` already works that way. vc-x1 doesn't know how to test; it runs the project's list in order, stops at the first failure, and says which command failed. `build` is the same, plus one check: the binary is where the config says. With the lists, `install` fits that too:

- **The project supplies how:** `[build] release`, `[install] release` (sign, package, copy to another machine), in its own checked-in scripts.
- **vc-x1 supplies the order and the checks:**
  - it always builds before it installs
  - the report says exactly which binary, which commit, and whether it's clean
  - it refuses a copy that would be wrong
  - `--dry-run` shows the report and touches nothing
  - the dev build can't land on the release's name

  Those are the mistakes we actually make, such as this morning's `cargo run install` onto the PATH, or the 39-line duplicate I left in the record. Writing them into each project's script wouldn't prevent them.
- **The built-in copy is only a default:** it's the common case done safely, rename-in-place included, so most projects need no script at all.

By that line vc-x1 isn't a build system. It doesn't know any build tool, it doesn't track staleness, and it doesn't define steps. It's closer to a checklist that runs itself. The cost is that it's one more layer to understand. The no-shell rule makes a list awkward to write, but that rule exists so exit statuses can't be masked, which is the same mistake-reducing reason.

So I'd keep the lists, as built. I'd also write that line into the cycle record's Deliberation, since it's the answer to this morning's question as much as the stamp was: "vc-x1 runs the project's steps in order and checks their results; the project says what the steps are." If it holds up, it could later go into `rationale.md`.

Should I add that Deliberation bullet and then commit this rung as is?

The plain version: vc-x1 shouldn't know how to install things, but it should make sure the install happens in the right order on the right binary, which is where mistakes come from. The lists let each project say how, and vc-x1 keeps the guard rails.

message.content: but the release and dev lists for install weren't trivial lists, like build unless we use scripts, is that correct?

content.text:
Correct. A `[build]` list is trivial because it needs no inputs from vc-x1: `cargo build --release --locked` already knows where everything is. An install list needs two facts only vc-x1 has, the binary and the destination. With no shell, the only way to read them from the environment is a script.

They can be made trivial without a shell. vc-x1 would substitute placeholders into each argument after splitting on whitespace, then run it:

I like naming them by key. A list says exactly where each value comes from, there's no new vocabulary to learn, and the same rule could later serve any list, `[validate]` included. Three things need settling first, and the third is the important one:

- **Resolved values, not raw text:** `{install.release-dir}` has to be the value this run actually uses, with `--dir` applied, `~` expanded, and a relative path resolved. If it substituted the raw `"~/.cargo/bin"`, `install --dir tmp/bin` would still copy onto the PATH, which is the mistake `--dir` exists to prevent. So placeholders would mean "the resolved value for this run", limited to the keys the command resolves. Any other `{...}` would be an error.
- **`cp` into a directory isn't safe here:** `cp {build.release-bin} {install.release-dir}` keeps the name, but it writes over the old file in place. When the old binary is running, which it is when vc-x1 installs itself, that fails with "Text file busy". The safe form copies to a temporary file and renames it, and that needs the destination file name, not just the directory.
- **The dev build would overwrite the release:** `cp {build.dev-bin} {install.dev-dir}` lands as `~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1`, not `vc-x1-dev`. That's exactly the overwrite you were worried about. The `-dev` name isn't in any key; vc-x1 derives it.

So I'd use key-named placeholders for the inputs, plus one derived value for the destination file, the only value no key holds. Calling it `{dest}`:

[install]
release = ["cp {build.release-bin} {dest}.new", "mv {dest}.new {dest}"]
release-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
dev = ["cp {build.dev-bin} {dest}.new", "mv {dest}.new {dest}"]
dev-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
```

`{dest}` is `{install.release-dir}/vc-x1` for `install` and `{install.dev-dir}/vc-x1-dev` for `install-dev`, with `--dir` applied. Both lists are equivalent to the built-in copy and need no script. `{install.release-dir}` stays available for a list that wants just the directory.

content.text:
On Windows, `copy` and `move` aren't programs. They're built into `cmd.exe`, so with no shell there's nothing for `{copy-cmd}` to resolve to. It would have to be `cmd /c copy`, which brings back a shell, and keeping the shell out is the reason lists split on whitespace. Two more Windows problems:

- **A running `.exe` can't be replaced in place on Windows,** even by renaming over it. The working method is to rename the running one aside, then move the new one in. vc-x1's built-in copy doesn't do that either: Rust's `std::fs::rename` fails there for a binary in use.
- **vc-x1 isn't Windows-ready today anyway.** The binary would be `vc-x1.exe`, `symlink` is `#[cfg(unix)]`, and `install_cmd`'s tests use `std::os::unix` unconditionally, so the crate's tests don't build on Windows.

I think this points the other way from `{copy-cmd}`. The portable copy belongs in vc-x1's built-in copy, which is Rust and the same on every platform; on Windows it would gain the rename-aside step. The lists are for the other ways of installing (signing, packaging, another machine), and those tools are platform-specific anyway, so a project's own script per platform is the honest form. No portable command vocabulary would be needed.

So I'd suggest:
- **This rung:** key-named placeholders as in my last message, with the environment variables dropped. No `{copy-cmd}`.
- **Todo entry:** "vc-x1 runs on Windows": the `.exe` names, the rename-aside install, and the unix-only code and tests.

content.text:
Yes. Windows finds programs through `PATHEXT`, so typing `vc-x1` runs `vc-x1.exe` from the PATH, the same as `cargo` runs `cargo.exe`. Users would type the same commands.

The file names carry the `.exe`, though, and three places would need to know:

- **Cargo's output:** `target/release/vc-x1.exe` and `target/debug/vc-x1.exe`. Today's `release-bin = "target/release/vc-x1"` would name a file that doesn't exist there. The config would need to say `.exe`, or vc-x1 would add the platform's suffix itself (Rust has `std::env::consts::EXE_SUFFIX`, which is `.exe` on Windows and empty elsewhere).
- **The `-dev` name:** `dest_name` adds `-dev` after the whole file name, so on Windows it would produce `vc-x1.exe-dev`, which Windows won't run. It needs to go before the extension: `vc-x1-dev.exe`. That's a small fix to the file-stem-plus-extension form, and it's correct on Linux too, where there's no extension.
- **The banner:** it takes its name from how the binary was run. It might show `vc-x1.exe` or `vc-x1`, depending on how Windows passes `argv[0]`.

I'd put all of that in the Windows Todo entry, beside the rename-aside install.

The plain version: yes, you'd still type `vc-x1`. The files would be `vc-x1.exe` and `vc-x1-dev.exe`, and the config and the `-dev` naming would need to handle the `.exe`.

content.text:
Yes, it would, if a `cp.exe` were on the PATH. Rust's `Command::new("cp")` on Windows searches the PATH and adds `.exe` when the name has none. That's narrower than `PATHEXT`: it finds `cp.exe`, but not a `cp.bat` or `cp.cmd`.

The catch is that Windows doesn't ship a `cp.exe`. One is there only if something installed it:
- Git for Windows, in `usr\bin`
- MSYS2 or Cygwin
- uutils coreutils

So a list written with `cp` and `mv` works on a Windows machine with one of those on the PATH, and fails elsewhere with the program not found. That fails loudly and is easy to read, but it's a dependency the project has to state.

The replace-a-running-binary problem holds even with `cp.exe`: on Windows, `mv` onto a running `vc-x1.exe` fails, so an equivalent list there needs the rename-aside step.

The plain version: yes, `cp` would find `cp.exe`, but only on Windows machines where something like Git for Windows installed it.

### vc-x1 runs on Windows

(wink + agent, 2026-10-22) vc-x1 builds and runs on Linux and macOS only. Weighed at the review
of the rung **feat: vc-x1 install-dev puts the dev build on the PATH**, in the cycle **feat: vc-x1
install stages, deploys, and runs builds**, when the install lists were written with `cp` and
`mv`. On Windows the binary is `vc-x1.exe`, run as `vc-x1`, and what follows from that is
unwritten.

- The binaries: cargo leaves `target/release/vc-x1.exe`, so `[build] release-bin` and `dev-bin`
  name the `.exe`, or vc-x1 adds `std::env::consts::EXE_SUFFIX` itself, a decision.
- The `-dev` name goes before the extension, `vc-x1-dev.exe`. `dest_name` in
  `src/install_cmd.rs` appends it to the whole file name, `vc-x1.exe-dev`, which Windows will not
  run.
- The built-in copy: a running `.exe` cannot be replaced in place, even by a rename over it, so
  the copy renames the running one aside and moves the new one in.
- The install lists: `cp` and `mv` exist on Windows only where something installed them, Git for
  Windows or MSYS2, and `copy` and `move` are `cmd.exe` builtins, not programs a list can run. A
  portable form, a `{cp}` placeholder, would be additive, since an unknown placeholder is an error
  today, and it resolves to a real program, perhaps vc-x1's own copy.
- The code: `symlink` is `#[cfg(unix)]`, and `install_cmd`'s tests use `std::os::unix`
  unconditionally, so the crate's tests do not build on Windows.

s=open(p).read()

b=s.index("- The help, the README's overview, table, config notes, the `install` section's list paragraph,")
new='''- `[install] release` and `dev` make the install scriptable as the build is: optional command
  lists that, when present, run in place of the built-in copy, after the same build, report, and
  refusals. Optional, not required as the build lists are, since the built-in copy is a default
  that needs no list. A dry run runs no list.
- The list's inputs are placeholders named by key, wink's call: `{build.release-bin}` and
  `{install.release-dir}`, or the `dev` pair, filled in each word after the whitespace split, so a
  value with spaces stays one word and no shell is added. Each is the value resolved for the run,
  `~` expanded and `--dir` applied, `--dir` made absolute, since otherwise `install --dir tmp/bin`
  would still write to the PATH. A `{name}` the command does not read is an error before the
  build. The first form, three `VC_X1_INSTALL_*` variables, needed a script for any use, since a
  list has no shell, and went.
- Weighed and set aside: a derived `{dest}`, the file name only vc-x1 knows, since with key-named
  placeholders the list names every path it writes and the user has the control, the `-dev` name
  included. The cost, accepted: a `dev` list that writes the release's name into a shared
  directory replaces the release, and vc-x1 cannot see it.
- This workspace sets both lists, wink's call, each the built-in copy written out, `cp` to a
  `.new` file and `mv` into place, safe over a running binary, so the config says what `install`
  does and the list path runs at every Land. The model's example is the same list, so a copied
  table works. `cp` and `mv` are not portable, and a `{cp}` placeholder would be additive later,

  caller, none for `validate` and `build`, whose lists are taken as written. The log shows each
  command with its placeholders filled, so it names the paths used. Clippy's register entry 5
  widens to the install lists.
- With a list the report's first line says `-> list` and the key, since vc-x1 no longer knows the

content.text:
It's in `src/command_list.rs:89-150`, three functions:

- **`words`** (`src/command_list.rs:110`): splits a command on whitespace, then fills each word separately, which is why a value with spaces stays one argument. With no `vars`, which is the `validate` and `build` case, words are taken as written.
- **`fill`** (`src/command_list.rs:123`): one word. It scans for `{`.
  - **Placeholder:** a name of letters, digits, `.`, `-`, `_`, immediately followed by `}`. It must be one of `vars`, or the error names the ones offered.
  - **Anything else is literal:** `{}`, `{` with no matching `}`, or a name containing other characters.
  - **Slicing is safe:** the indices come from `find` on ASCII characters (`{`, `}`, and the first non-name character), so every slice falls on a character boundary.
- **`check_placeholders`** (`src/command_list.rs:91`): runs `words` with empty values, purely to catch unknown names before anything runs.

Where they're used:
- **`run_one`** (`src/command_list.rs:203`): calls `words` to get the program and its arguments.
- **`run`** (`src/command_list.rs:169`): calls it again to print the filled command in the log.
- **`install_params`** (`src/install_cmd.rs:221`): calls `check_placeholders` before the build.
- **`run_list`** (`src/install_cmd.rs:558`): builds the two `(name, value)` pairs from the resolved binary and directory.

The tests are `placeholders_fill_words` in the same file.

content.text:
Yes. Only `install` and `install-dev` offer placeholders, two each:

| Command | List | Placeholders |
|---|---|---|
| `install` | `[install] release` | `{build.release-bin}`, `{install.release-dir}` |
| `install-dev` | `[install] dev` | `{build.dev-bin}`, `{install.dev-dir}` |
| `build`, `build-dev` | `[build] release`, `dev` | none |
| `validate` | `[validate] full`, `fast` | none |

`validate` and `build` pass an empty list of placeholders, so their commands run exactly as written. A `{...}` in them stays literal and isn't an error. That keeps every existing list unchanged.

The mechanism is general, so another list could offer placeholders later by passing its own pairs; for example, the run rung's `run` could offer `{build.release-bin}`. Each command offers only the keys it actually resolves, and nothing reads arbitrary config keys.

The plain version: yes, only the install lists fill in `{...}` today. The others run as written.

message.content: Any reason not to allow everyone including other apps to use it?

content.text:
No strong reason against. Two things need settling to do it right.

- **What a placeholder means outside its command:** `{install.release-dir}` inside `install` is the value with `--dir` applied, resolved and absolute. In a `[validate]` list there's no `--dir`, so it would be the configured value, resolved the same way. That's consistent if the rule is "the value as this run resolves it". The harder part is arbitrary keys: the four path keys need resolving (`~` expanded, relative to the config's directory), and the schema doesn't mark which keys are paths, since they're all `kind = "str"`. So "any config key" would need a `path` kind in the schema first, or vc-x1 would substitute raw text for some keys and resolved paths for others. That mixing is the trap we avoided with `--dir`.
- **Existing lists:** with placeholders offered everywhere, a literal `{name}` in an existing `[validate]` or `[build]` list becomes an error.
  - `{}`, as in `find -exec ... {} \;`, stays literal because the name is empty.
  - None of this workspace's lists has braces.
  - Another project's might, but it fails loudly at the first run, naming the word, never silently.

"Other apps" come for free: placeholders are part of vc-x1's config, so any project using vc-x1 gets them in its own lists.

My suggestion is to make it uniform, with a fixed set:
- **Every list can use them:** `[validate]`, `[build]`, `[install]`, and later `[run]`.
- **The set is the four path keys:** `{build.release-bin}`, `{build.dev-bin}`, `{install.release-dir}`, `{install.dev-dir}`, each resolved. `--dir` applies only to the install command running.
- **A key that isn't set is an error naming it.**
- **Other keys later:** they come when the schema can say which keys are paths.

One example of the use: `[validate] full` could end with `"{build.dev-bin} -V"` as a smoke check.

That widens this rung again. Should I do it here, or put it in the run rung, where `[run]` needs the same thing?

message.content: Seems to me any string being assigned to any table field should be able to use them?

content.text:
I'd push back on that one, though not on the idea of placeholders everywhere in lists.

A placeholder in a plain string value is a different feature from one in a command list. Say `dev-dir = "{install.release-dir}"`, or `release-bin = "target/release/{package.name}"`:

- **They need two different meanings:**
  - **In a command list:** `{install.release-dir}` has to be the resolved value for the run, absolute with `--dir` applied, because nothing after vc-x1 will resolve it.
  - **In a config value:** it has to be the other key's raw text, `~/.cargo/bin`, because the receiving key resolves its own value. If it substituted the resolved path, `dev-dir` would get a path with `--dir` baked in, or one resolved against the wrong directory.

  Same syntax, two meanings, and the user has to know which applies where. That's the trap.
- **It becomes a small templating language:**
  - Values can refer to values, so references need ordering and cycle detection (`a = "{b}"`, `b = "{a}"`).
  - A literal brace in any value needs an escape.
  - It reaches every config reader: `repos.*`, `agent-session.*`, the user config, the agent side's config. All of them read the config through one loader, so the change would be global, and the user config and the workspace config are separate files with their own rules about which keys belong where.

  That's the "it gets complicated" feeling from this morning, and it adds no check that prevents a mistake.
- **No current need:** nothing in this cycle wants one value to refer to another. The need we have is commands knowing paths, and list placeholders cover that.

So I'd draw the line here:
- **Command lists:** placeholders in every list, `[validate]`, `[build]`, `[install]`, and later `[run]`, with the four path keys resolved, as in my last message.
- **Plain values:** no placeholders. If one config value ever needs another, that's its own Todo entry, designed with the escape and the cycle rules.

Do you agree with that line? And if so, should the every-list part go in this rung or the run rung?

content.text: What defines a "Command list" is that list hard coded to a particular file?

lastPrompt: What defines a "Command list" is that list hard coded to a particular file?

content.text:
Code defines it, not a file. A command list is a `str-list` config key that some subcommand hands to `command_list::run`. Each subcommand names its own keys in its source:

| Keys | Hard-coded in | Run by |
|---|---|---|
| `validate.full`, `validate.fast` | `src/validate.rs` | `validate` |
| `build.release`, `build.dev` | `src/build_cmd.rs` | `build`, `build-dev` |
| `install.release`, `install.dev` | `src/install_cmd.rs` | `install`, `install-dev` |

All six are read from the work side's config, found from the workspace root by `config_md::load`; here that's `.vc-config.md`. The schema (`vc-config.md`) declares them `kind = "str-list"`, and right now those six are the only `str-list` keys. But that kind describes a shape, a TOML array of strings, not "a list of commands". Nothing in the schema says a key is run.

So "placeholders in every command list" would be true by convention: these six, plus whatever key a future subcommand passes to `command_list::run`. To make it one definition, the schema could mark them with `kind = "command-list"`. Then the rule "a command list's words take placeholders" lives in one place, and `config --validate` could check a list's placeholders without running it. That would fit beside a `path` kind, if config values ever get placeholders.

The plain version: there's no special file; a "command list" is any list in `.vc-config.md` that some vc-x1 command runs, and each command names its own lists in code.

content.text:
Nothing changes for command lists or placeholders. Both names are valid carriers, and `config_md::vc_config_path` (`src/config_md.rs:33`) picks whichever one exists:

- **`.vc-config.md`:** only the fences tagged exactly `toml` are read, joined in order, and the prose around them is skipped.
- **`.vc-config.toml`:** read as plain TOML.
- **Both present:** an error, and nothing is changed.

Either way, `load_file` produces the same flat map of keys (`install.release`, `build.dev-bin`, ...). The commands, `command_list`, and the placeholders only ever see that map, never the file. So which keys are command lists, and which placeholders they accept, is the same under either name.

The rename alone isn't enough, though. The file's content has to become plain TOML: keep the bodies of the `toml` fences, in order, and drop the prose, the `[[N]]` links, and their reference lines. A `.toml` file still holding Markdown prose isn't valid TOML. I haven't checked what vc-x1's lenient parser does with such lines, so I won't claim it would fail cleanly. The cost is losing the documentation beside each table, which is why `.vc-config.md` is the current carrier.

The plain version: the file name doesn't matter to command lists; both names give vc-x1 the same keys. A `.toml` file just has to hold plain TOML, without the explanations.

message.content: So [repos], [remote] and [family] can't use them and they can't be referenced in a string in [validate], [build], [install] or [run]

content.text:
Yes. Under the line I proposed, both are true:

- **They can't use placeholders:** `[repos]`, `[remote]`, and `[family]` hold plain values, and a `{...}` in a plain value stays literal text.
- **They can't be referenced:** a command list can name only the four path keys, `build.release-bin`, `build.dev-bin`, `install.release-dir`, and `install.dev-dir`. Today the code is narrower still: only the install lists, two keys each.

The second limit is the softer one. Nothing in the mechanism stops a list from naming more keys; each key just needs a defined value. Most of those tables are paths vc-x1 already resolves:

| Key | Value | Resolved by vc-x1 |
|---|---|---|
| `repos.work`, `repos.agent` | paths | yes, against the config's directory |
| `family.member`, `family.template`, `family.messages` | paths | yes |
| `remote.agent-repo` | a name, not a path | none needed; the raw text |
| `test.fixtures` | a path | yes |

So the referenceable set could be "every key vc-x1 resolves, each as it resolves it". For example, a `[validate]` list could run something against `{repos.agent}`. The cost is that each key needs its resolution stated once, which a `path` kind in the schema would do.

The first limit, plain values using placeholders, is the one I'd keep out for now. It's what turns the config into a templating language, with the raw-or-resolved ambiguity and the cycles.

Would you like the referenceable set widened to every resolved key? If so, should it go in this rung or the run rung?

message.content: In my opinion, if a string being assigned to some table entries can reference any table entry then "some" should be "any" too?

content.text:
You're right that it's the cleaner rule, and my main objection goes away. I argued that a placeholder would need two meanings, raw text in plain values and the resolved value in lists. It doesn't, if two things hold:

- **A reference always means the resolved value:** `{install.release-dir}` is `/home/wink/.cargo/bin`, absolute, wherever it appears. That works in a plain value too. `dev-dir = "{install.release-dir}"` gets an absolute path, and an absolute path is a valid value for `dev-dir`, so resolving it again changes nothing. Keys that aren't paths, like `remote.agent-repo`, resolve to their own text.
- **`--dir` is an override of the key, not a special case in the list:** `install --dir tmp/bin` means "`install.release-dir` is `tmp/bin`, absolute, for this run", applied to the config before references are filled. Then everything that names the key sees the same value, lists and plain values alike.

With those, "any string can reference any key" is one rule. What it still takes:

- **Which keys are paths:** a `path` kind in the schema, so vc-x1 knows to resolve those. Their resolution already exists in each reader.
- **One pass in the loader:** references filled once at load, so every command reads finished values. Cycles (`a = "{b}"`, `b = "{a}"`) and unknown names are errors naming the keys. A brace that isn't a placeholder (`{}`, `{a b}`) stays literal, as now.
- **Scope:** a reference stays within its own file, the workspace config or the user config. The two have separate homes for their keys.
- **Every reader at once:** `repos`, `family`, `agent-session`, and the rest all see filled values. That's the point, but it also means it's a change to config loading, not to install.

That's a cycle-sized change to the config loader and schema, well beyond `install-dev`. So I'd suggest:
- **This rung:** keep what's built, the install lists with their two keys each. It's a strict subset of the general rule, so nothing written now would need to change later.
- **A Todo entry, "Any config string references any key":** the design above, as its own cycle.

Does that work, or do you want the general rule before this rung lands?

message.content: I think the "-dev" trailer should be in vc-config maybe in the [build] table?

content.text:
I think a key makes sense, but I'd put it in `[install]`, not `[build]`. Nothing in the build uses the suffix: the dev build leaves `target/debug/vc-x1`, no suffix. The only place `-dev` is added is the install-dev copy, when it names the file in `dev-dir`. A `[build]` key would suggest the build produces `vc-x1-dev`, and it doesn't.

My proposal:

```toml
[install]
release = [...]
release-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
dev = [...]
dev-dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
dev-suffix = "-dev"
```

- **Default `-dev`:** a workspace that doesn't set it gets today's behavior. The schema would carry `default = "-dev"`, unlike the directory keys, which have no sensible default.
- **Who reads it:** the built-in copy uses it to name the file (`vc-x1` + `dev-suffix`). The `dev` list could use it too as `{install.dev-suffix}`: `{install.dev-dir}/vc-x1{install.dev-suffix}`. That adds a third key to install-dev's placeholders, which fits the general Todo rule.
- **A guard it makes possible:** with an empty suffix and `dev-dir` the same as `release-dir`, the built-in copy would replace the release. `install-dev` can refuse whenever its destination equals `install`'s, naming both keys. That restores the protection the fixed suffix gave, and it covers `--dir` landing on the release's directory as well. It can't cover a list, which writes where it says.
- **This workspace's lists:** they'd use `{install.dev-suffix}` instead of writing `-dev` out, so the suffix is stated in one place.

This reverses the fixed-suffix call, so I'm stopping to check: `[install] dev-suffix`, defaulting to `-dev`, with the guard and the placeholder, in this rung?

content.content:
## install.dev-dir

The one directory `vc-x1 install-dev` copies the dev build into, as the file name
[build.dev-bin](#builddev-bin) gives it with `-dev` appended, so it may be the release's own
directory, [install.release-dir](#installrelease-dir), and the dev build sits beside the release
there without replacing it. Expanded as `install.release-dir` is. A workspace without the key has
no dev build to install, and `vc-x1 install-dev` says so. `--dir` replaces it for one run. Owned
by the work side because it deploys the artifact.

```toml
[install.dev-dir]
homes = ["workspace-code"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Where `vc-x1 install-dev` copies the dev build as <name>-dev, `~` expanded"
used-by = "vc-x1 install-dev"
example = "~/.cargo/bin"
```

release's, as an empty suffix in that directory or a `--dir` onto it would make it. A list writes
where it says, so it names the suffix itself, `{install.dev-suffix}`, as this workspace's does.

content.text:
For the commands this cycle touches, here is what each one needs from the config. Everything is checked before anything runs.

| Command | Needs | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| `validate` | `[validate] full` (or `fast` with `--fast`) | none |
| `build` | `[build] release`, `[build] release-bin` | none |
| `build-dev` | `[build] dev` | none (`dev-bin` isn't read) |
| `install` | everything `build` needs, plus `[install] release-dir` | `[install] release` |
| `install-dev` | everything `build-dev` needs, plus `[build] dev-bin` and `[install] dev-dir` | `[install] dev`, `[install] dev-suffix` (defaults to `-dev`) |

`--dir` takes the place of `release-dir` or `dev-dir` for a run, so with `--dir` those two aren't needed.

**iiac-perf with this version:** its config has `[repos]`, `[family]`, and `[validate]`, and no `[build]` or `[install]`.
- `validate` works as before; nothing about it changed. Its `full` list ends with `cargo install --path . --locked`, and that still runs.
- `build`/`build-dev` stop with `no \`build.release\` table` (or `build.dev`), telling you to add one.
- `install`/`install-dev` stop on the missing `release-dir`/`dev-dir`, before building, as in your run.

So nothing that iiac-perf uses today breaks. The new commands need their tables added; until then they refuse instead of guessing.

**A plain repo with no `.vc-config.md` (or `.vc-config.toml`):** none of these five commands has a workspace without a config. Each stops with `not in a vc-x1 workspace (no config found)`, before running anything. The banner still prints, just without the agent-files suffix. vc-x1 knows where it is only from a config file; it never guesses from the current directory.

That's as far as I've checked. Other commands (`status`, `commit`, `push`, `sync`, `-s p`) have their own rules about whether they need a config. There's a test, `resolve_scoped_repos_por_refuses_a_side_and_takes_a_plain_repo`, which suggests `-s p` works on a plain repo, but I haven't audited the commands one by one. If you want the full list, I can go through every subcommand and write up what each needs; that's a read across most of `src/`.

The plain version: the build and install commands each need their own config table and refuse clearly without it. iiac-perf keeps working for what it uses now, and a repo with no config gets a clear "not a workspace" error from these commands.

The two working-copy items are still open: `[install]` is commented out, and `vc-x1` is at the repo root.
